questions.question: The chapter's epigraph asks 'Is it better to be alive and wrong or right and dead?' Who wrote it, and which trade-off is it a compressed statement of?

options.text: Jay Kreps, A Few Notes on Kafka and Jepsen (2013) — a compressed statement of the choice between staying available and honouring the recency guarantee, which the chapter develops under The Cost of Linearizability and the CAP theorem
Eric Brewer, Towards Robust Distributed Systems (2000) — about partition tolerance
Leslie Lamport, The Part-Time Parliament (1998) — about Paxos
Kyle Kingsbury, Jepsen analyses (2013) — about testing

questions.explanation: 'Alive and wrong' is the available-but-stale branch; 'right and dead' is the linearizable-but-unavailable one.

questions.question: What does the chapter name as the simplest way of handling faults, and what is the alternative?

options.text: The simplest way is to simply let the entire service fail and show the user an error message. The alternative is tolerating faults — that is, keeping the service functioning correctly even if some internal component is faulty
The simplest way is retrying; the alternative is replication
The simplest way is failover; the alternative is manual repair
The simplest way is logging; the alternative is monitoring

questions.explanation: Fail loudly versus keep working — the chapter is about the second.

questions.question: Which Chapter 8 problems does the chapter assume can occur? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Packets can be lost, reordered, duplicated, or arbitrarily delayed in the network
Clocks are approximate at best
Nodes can pause for a considerable amount of time or crash at any time
Nodes may lie and send arbitrary faulty responses

questions.explanation: Byzantine behaviour is excluded — the chapter assumes non-Byzantine faults.

questions.question: What does the chapter call 'the best way of building fault-tolerant systems', and which pretenses did the transaction abstraction buy in Chapter 7? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Find some general-purpose abstractions with useful guarantees, implement them once, and then let applications rely on those guarantees
That there are no crashes (atomicity)
That nobody else is concurrently accessing the database (isolation)
That storage devices are perfectly reliable (durability)

questions.explanation: Even though crashes, race conditions, and disk failures do occur, the transaction abstraction hides those problems.

questions.question: Define consensus as the chapter's opening defines it, and give its verdict on difficulty.

options.text: Getting all of the nodes to agree on something — one of the most important abstractions for distributed systems. Reliably reaching consensus in spite of network faults and process failures is a surprisingly tricky problem
Electing a leader among a set of nodes, which is straightforward with timeouts
Ordering all writes in a replication log, which is solved by Lamport timestamps
Detecting node failures reliably, which is impossible

questions.explanation: Agreement on something, and it is surprisingly tricky.

questions.question: What concrete use of consensus does the opening give?

options.text: A database with single-leader replication that needs to fail over to a new leader if the old one dies can use consensus to elect a new leader — it's important that there is only one leader and that all nodes agree who the leader is, since otherwise a split brain can occur, which often leads to data loss
Deciding which partition a key belongs to
Deciding when to compact SSTables
Deciding the isolation level for a transaction

questions.explanation: Leader election, with split brain as the failure it prevents and data loss as the consequence.

questions.question: Put the chapter's three movements in order.

options.text: Linearizability, one of the strongest consistency models in common use; then ordering guarantees, particularly around causality and total ordering; then distributed transactions and consensus. The three areas are in fact deeply linked
Consensus, then linearizability, then ordering
Ordering, then consensus, then linearizability
Transactions, then replication, then partitioning

questions.explanation: The chapter's point is that these are not three separate topics but one.

questions.question: Why does the chapter map fundamental limits rather than jumping to algorithms?

options.text: Because in some situations it's possible for the system to tolerate faults and continue working, while in other situations that is not possible — and the limits of what is and isn't possible have been explored in depth, both in theoretical proofs and in practical implementations
Because algorithms change too often to be worth learning
Because proofs are more useful than implementations
Because the chapter has no space for algorithms

questions.explanation: The chapter also states its self-limitation: it can only scratch the surface, will not go into details of formal models and proofs, and sticks with informal intuitions, pointing to the literature references for depth.

questions.question: Why do you see different data on two database nodes at the same moment, and which replication methods does this affect?

options.text: Because write requests arrive on different nodes at different times — and these inconsistencies occur no matter what replication method the database uses: single-leader, multi-leader or leaderless
Because of clock skew; only leaderless replication is affected
Because of partitioning; only multi-leader replication is affected
Because of network faults; only single-leader replication is affected

questions.explanation: Arrival-time differences, and no replication method escapes them.

questions.question: State the definition of eventual consistency exactly, including the two qualifiers readers usually drop.

options.text: If you stop writing to the database and wait for some unspecified length of time, then eventually all read requests will return the same value
All reads return the latest write within a bounded time
All replicas converge within one second of a write
All reads on the same node return the same value

questions.explanation: You must stop writing, and the waiting time is unspecified. The parenthetical assumption is that any conflicts are resolved. The chapter suggests 'convergence' would be a better name, as we expect all replicas to eventually converge to the same value.

questions.question: What does the chapter say eventual consistency does not promise? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: It doesn't say anything about when the replicas will converge
Until the time of convergence, reads could return anything or nothing
There is no guarantee that you will see the value you just wrote
It does not guarantee durability of writes

questions.explanation: Three specific complaints. Read-your-writes is separately discussed in Chapter 5.

questions.question: Why is eventual consistency specifically hard for application developers?

options.text: Because it is so different from the behavior of variables in a normal single-threaded program: if you write a value to a variable and then read it shortly afterwards you don't expect to read back the old value, or for the read to fail. A database looks superficially like a variable that you can read and write, but in fact it has much more complicated semantics
Because the API is unfamiliar
Because it requires manual conflict resolution in every case
Because it cannot be tested

questions.explanation: The variable analogy is what makes the weak semantics surprising.

questions.question: Why are weak-guarantee bugs subtle and hard to find by testing?

options.text: Because when working with a database that provides only weak guarantees you need to be constantly aware of its limitations and not accidentally assume too much: bugs are often subtle, and the application may work well most of the time, with problems only becoming apparent when there is a fault in the system, such as a network interruption, or at high concurrency
Because they only occur in production
Because they always crash the application
Because tests cannot exercise a database

questions.explanation: Faults and high concurrency are the two conditions that surface them.

questions.question: What do stronger guarantees cost, and what do they buy?

options.text: Systems with stronger guarantees may have worse performance or be less fault-tolerant than systems with weaker guarantees — but in exchange they are easier to use correctly
They cost only money; they buy correctness
They cost nothing and buy correctness
They cost correctness and buy performance

questions.explanation: Performance and fault tolerance traded for ease of correct use.

questions.question: How does the chapter separate distributed consistency models from transaction isolation levels?

options.text: While there is some overlap, they are mostly independent concerns: transaction isolation is primarily about avoiding race conditions due to concurrently executing transactions, whereas distributed consistency is mostly about coordinating the state of replicas in the face of delays and faults
They are the same hierarchy under two names
Isolation is a special case of consistency
Consistency is a special case of isolation

questions.explanation: Concurrency versus replication — mostly independent, with some overlap.

questions.question: What is the wish that motivates linearizability, and what other names does it go by? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The wish: to make a system appear as if there were only one replica, so that every client would have the same view of the data and you don't have to worry about replication lag
It is also known as atomic consistency and strong consistency
It is also known as immediate consistency and external consistency
It is also known as eventual consistency

questions.explanation: Four other names in the literature — though the exact definition is quite subtle.

questions.question: Walk Figure 9-1.

options.text: Alice and Bob are sitting in the same room, both checking their phones to see the outcome of the 2014 FIFA World Cup final. Just after the final score is announced, Alice reloads the page, sees the winner, and excitedly tells Bob. Bob incredulously hits reload on his own phone, but his request goes to a database replica that is lagging, and so his phone shows that the game is still ongoing. This system is not linearizable, causing football fans to be confused
Two clients write conflicting values and the database keeps both
A leader fails and a stale follower is promoted
A transaction reads a partially updated state

questions.explanation: A stale read that is provably stale because of an out-of-band channel.

questions.question: What precisely converts Bob's stale read into a linearizability violation?

options.text: That Bob knows he hit the reload button — initiated his query — after he heard Alice exclaim the final score, so he expects the result of his query to be at least as recent as Alice's. If they had hit reload at the same instant and gotten different answers it would have been less surprising, because they wouldn't know at exactly what time their respective requests were processed by the server
That the replica was lagging by more than one second
That both requests went to different replicas
That the score had already been written to disk

questions.explanation: The known ordering between the two reads is what makes the staleness a violation.

questions.question: In Figure 9-2, what is x called in the literature, and what could it be?

options.text: A register — in practice it could be one key in a key-value store, one row in a relational database, or one document in a document database
A variable — in practice a table, an index, or a partition
An object — in practice a transaction, a lock, or a lease
A replica — in practice a node, a disk, or a file

questions.explanation: Linearizability is defined over a single register at a time.

questions.question: In Figures 9-2 through 9-4, what do the ends of each bar mean?

options.text: The start of a bar is the time when the request was sent and the end of a bar is when the response was received by the client. Because of variable network delays the client doesn't know exactly when the database processed its request — it only knows that it happened sometime between the client sending the request and receiving the response
The start is when the database processed the request and the end is when it was durable
The start is the transaction begin and the end is the commit
The bars show the duration of the network round-trip only

questions.explanation: A footnote flags a subtle detail: the diagram assumes the existence of a global clock, represented by the horizontal axis. For the purposes of analyzing a distributed algorithm we may pretend an accurate global clock exists, as long as the algorithm doesn't have access to it — the algorithm only gets a mangled approximation of real time, as produced by a quartz oscillator and NTP.

questions.question: In Figure 9-2, x is initially 0 and client C writes 1 while A and B poll. Which are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A read that completes before the write begins must return the old value 0
A read that begins after the write has completed must return the new value 1
A read that overlaps the write in time may return either 0 or 1, because we don't know whether the write has taken effect at the point when the read is processed — these operations are concurrent
A read that overlaps the write must return 1

questions.explanation: Rule (c) alone is insufficient: it permits the value to flip back and forth between old and new across successive reads. A footnote notes that a register that allows exactly that is called a regular register.

questions.question: What extra constraint does Figure 9-3 add?

options.text: After any one read has returned the new value, all following reads — on the same or other clients — must also return the new value. The figure imagines the register atomically flipping from the old to the new value at some point, even if the write operation has not yet completed; the arrow shows that B's read occurs strictly after A's read
That reads must be served from the leader
That writes must be synchronous
That concurrent reads must return the same value

questions.explanation: This is the constraint that rules out flip-flopping.

questions.question: Define the third operation type introduced in Figure 9-4.

options.text: Compare-and-set: cas(x, v_old, v_new) means the client requested an atomic update. If the current value of the register x equals v_old, it should be atomically set to v_new; if x is not equal to v_old then the operation leaves the register unchanged and returns an error. The response r is ok or error
Increment-and-get, which adds one and returns the result
Read-modify-write, which is not atomic
Append, which adds to a log

questions.explanation: Compare-and-set is the operation that later turns out to require consensus.

questions.question: What do the vertical lines inside the bars in Figure 9-4 represent, and what must the joining lines satisfy?

options.text: Each operation is marked with a vertical line, inside its bar, at the time when we think the operation was executed. Those markers are joined up in sequential order, and the result must be a valid sequence of reads and writes for a register: every read must return the value set by the most recent write. The requirement of linearizability is that the lines joining up the operation markers always move forward in time, never backward
They mark the request send time; the lines may move backward
They mark durability; the lines are unordered
They mark network arrival; the lines must be evenly spaced

questions.explanation: Forward-only ordering ensures the recency guarantee: once a new value has been written or read, all subsequent reads see the value that was written, until it is overwritten again.

questions.question: In Figure 9-4, B sends its read first, then D sends set x = 0, then A sends set x = 1 — yet B's read returns 1. Why is this legal?

options.text: Because the database first processed D's write, then A's write, and finally B's read. Although this is not the order in which the requests were sent, it is an acceptable order, because the three requests are concurrent
Because reads are always served from the leader
It is not legal; the figure shows a violation here
Because B's read had a later timestamp

questions.explanation: Concurrent requests may be processed in any order, including one that differs from send order.

questions.question: B's read returns 1 before client A receives its ok confirming the write of 1. Why is this not a violation?

options.text: Because it doesn't mean the value was read before it was written — it just means the ok response from the database to client A was slightly delayed
Because reads and writes are independent operations
Because B read from a different replica
It is a violation, and the figure marks it as such

questions.explanation: The response delay is on the network, not in the execution order.

questions.question: Figure 9-4's model doesn't assume transaction isolation. How does that show up, and which cas requests succeed?

options.text: Another client may change a value at any time: client C first reads 1 and then reads 2, because the value was changed by B between the two reads. B and C's cas requests succeed, but D's cas request fails, because at the time when the database processes it the value of x is no longer 0
All three cas requests succeed
Only D's cas succeeds
All three cas requests fail

questions.explanation: No isolation means an intervening write can invalidate the compare.

questions.question: Which operation in Figure 9-4 is not linearizable, and why?

options.text: The final read by client B, shown in a shaded bar. It is concurrent with C's cas which updates x from 2 to 4, so in the absence of other requests it would be okay for B's read to return 2 — however, client A has already read the new value 4 before B's read started, so B is not allowed to read an older value than A
D's cas, because it returned an error
A's write of 1, because it overlapped D's write of 0
C's first read of 1, because it preceded the write

questions.explanation: Once a newer value has been read by anyone, no later read may go back. Testing for linearizability is possible but computationally expensive: you record the timings of all requests and responses and check whether they can be arranged into a valid sequential order.

questions.question: From the 'Linearizability Versus Serializability' box, define serializability.

options.text: Serializability is an isolation property of transactions, where every transaction may read and write multiple objects: it guarantees that transactions behave the same as if they had executed in some serial order, and it is okay for that serial order to be different from the order in which transactions were actually run
It is a recency guarantee on a single register
It requires the serial order to match the real-time order
It applies to single-object operations only

questions.explanation: Multiple objects, some serial order, and the order need not match reality.

questions.question: From the same box, define linearizability and name the anomaly it doesn't prevent.

options.text: Linearizability is a recency guarantee on reads and writes of an individual object — a key or register. It doesn't group operations together into transactions, so it does not prevent problems such as write skew unless you take additional measures such as materializing conflicts
It prevents write skew automatically
It groups operations into transactions
It applies across multiple objects

questions.explanation: Single object, recency only — write skew spans objects and so escapes it.

questions.question: What is the combination of serializability and linearizability called, and which implementations provide it?

options.text: Strict serializability, or strong one-copy serializability (strong-1SR). Implementations of serializability based on two-phase locking or actual serial execution are typically linearizable
Strong eventual consistency; provided by SSI
Snapshot serializability; provided by MVCC
Atomic serializability; provided by 2PC

questions.explanation: 2PL and serial execution give both; SSI does not.

questions.question: Which serializability implementation is not linearizable, and why by design?

options.text: Serializable snapshot isolation. By design it makes reads from a consistent snapshot to avoid lock contention between readers and writers, and the whole point of a consistent snapshot is that it does not include writes that are more recent than the snapshot — so reads from the snapshot are not linearizable
Two-phase locking, because locks are released early
Serial execution, because it runs on one thread
All serializable implementations are linearizable

questions.explanation: A consistent snapshot deliberately excludes recent writes, which is exactly what linearizability forbids.

questions.question: Which properties belong to linearizability rather than serializability? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: It is a recency guarantee
It concerns a single object or register
It is an isolation property of transactions spanning multiple objects
Its serial order may differ from the real execution order

questions.explanation: The last two belong to serializability. The chapter notes the words are easily confused, as both seem to mean 'can be arranged in a sequential order' — but they are two quite different guarantees.

questions.question: Describe the lock-based leader election scheme and its requirement.

options.text: Every node that starts up tries to acquire the lock, and the one that succeeds becomes the leader. No matter how this lock is implemented, it must be linearizable: all nodes must agree which node owns the lock, otherwise it is useless — so that there is indeed only one leader, not several, which would be split brain
The node with the lowest ID becomes leader; no lock is needed
All nodes become leaders and resolve conflicts later
The lock may be eventually consistent

questions.explanation: Without agreement on ownership, the lock provides nothing.

questions.question: Which coordination services does the chapter name, and what sits on top?

options.text: Apache ZooKeeper and etcd, which use consensus algorithms to implement linearizable operations in a fault-tolerant way. There are still many subtle details to implementing locks and leader election correctly — for example the fencing issue — and libraries like Apache Curator help by providing higher-level recipes on top of ZooKeeper. But a linearizable storage service is the basic foundation for these coordination tasks
Redis and Memcached, with Curator on top
Consul and Kafka, with ZooKeeper on top
Cassandra and Riak, with Helix on top

questions.explanation: A footnote adds the fine print: strictly speaking ZooKeeper and etcd provide linearizable writes, but reads may be stale since by default they can be served by any one of the replicas — in etcd you can request a quorum read, and in ZooKeeper you need to call sync() before the read.

questions.question: Describe distributed locking in Oracle Real Application Clusters.

options.text: RAC uses a lock per disk page, with multiple nodes sharing access to the same disk storage system. Since these linearizable locks are on the critical path of transaction execution, RAC deployments usually have a dedicated cluster interconnect network for communication between database nodes
It uses a lock per table over the public network
It uses a lock per transaction with no shared storage
It uses no locks; it relies on MVCC

questions.explanation: Page-granularity locks on the critical path force a dedicated interconnect.

questions.question: Give the chapter's examples of uniqueness constraints, and when linearizability becomes necessary.

options.text: A username or email address must uniquely identify one user, and in a file storage service there cannot be two files with the same path and filename. If you want to enforce this constraint as the data is written — such that if two people concurrently try to create a user or a file with the same name, one of them will be returned an error — you need linearizability
Foreign key constraints; linearizability is needed for all constraints
Range constraints; linearizability is never needed
Check constraints; linearizability is needed only on read

questions.explanation: Enforcement at write time is what requires linearizability.

questions.question: How does the chapter reframe username registration?

options.text: As similar to a lock: when a user registers for your service you can think of them acquiring a 'lock' on their chosen username. The operation is also very similar to an atomic compare-and-set, setting the username to the ID of the user who claimed it, provided that the username is not already taken
As a foreign key reference
As an eventual-consistency merge
As a read-only query

questions.explanation: Lock and compare-and-set are two framings of the same requirement.

questions.question: Which further examples of single-value constraints does the chapter give, and what is the common property? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A bank account balance never going negative
Not selling more items than you have in stock
Two people not concurrently booking the same seat on a flight or in a theater
Referential integrity between two tables

questions.explanation: These constraints all require there to be a single up-to-date value — the account balance, the stock level, the seat occupancy — that all nodes agree on.

questions.question: Give the chapter's example of a constraint treated loosely.

options.text: Constraints can be treated loosely if the application can easily handle the violation after the fact: for example if a flight is overbooked you can move customers to a different flight and offer them compensation for the inconvenience — in which case linearizability may not be needed. The chapter defers the topic to Timeliness and Integrity
Bank balances, which can go negative temporarily with no consequence
Usernames, which can be duplicated and merged
File paths, which can collide safely

questions.explanation: Compensatable violations don't need prevention. The chapter draws a sharp line: a hard uniqueness constraint such as the one typically found in relational databases requires linearizability, whereas other kinds of constraints such as foreign key or attribute constraints can be implemented without requiring linearizability.

questions.question: In Figure 9-1, what would have happened if Alice had said nothing?

options.text: Bob wouldn't have known that the result of his query was stale. The linearizability violation was only noticed because there was an additional communication channel in the system — Alice's voice to Bob's ears
The database would have detected and reported the staleness
Bob would have seen the correct result
The replica would have blocked the read

questions.explanation: Without the out-of-band channel, staleness is undetectable to the client.

questions.question: Describe the photo-upload architecture of Figure 9-5, and why the photo isn't put on the queue.

options.text: A web server handles uploads and a background process resizes the photos to lower resolution for faster download (thumbnails). The resizer needs to be explicitly instructed to perform a resizing job, and this instruction is sent from the web server to the resizer via a message queue. The web server doesn't place the entire photo on the queue, since most message brokers are designed for small messages and a photo may be several megabytes in size — instead the photo is first written to a file storage service, and once that write is complete the instruction to the resizer is placed on the queue, opening the potential for race conditions
The photo is placed on the queue because brokers handle large messages well
The photo is written to the resizer's local disk
There is no message queue; the web server calls the resizer directly

questions.explanation: Two channels — file storage and message queue — is what creates the race.

questions.question: If the file storage service in Figure 9-5 is not linearizable, what can go wrong?

options.text: There is a risk of a race condition: the message queue might be faster than the internal replication inside the storage service, so when the resizer fetches the image at step 5 it might see an old version of the image, or nothing at all. If it processes an old version, the full-size and resized images in the file storage become permanently inconsistent
The queue message is lost and the photo is never resized
The photo is resized twice, wasting CPU
Nothing; the resizer will retry until correct

questions.explanation: Permanent inconsistency is what distinguishes this from Alice's self-correcting reload.

questions.question: State the general shape of the cross-channel problem and the alternative to linearizability.

options.text: The problem arises because there are two different communication channels between the web server and the resizer — the file storage and the message queue — so without the recency guarantee of linearizability, race conditions between these two channels are possible. This is analogous to Figure 9-1, where the two channels were database replication and the real-life audio channel. Linearizability is not the only way of avoiding this race condition, but it's the simplest to understand; if you control the additional communication channel you can use alternative approaches similar to those discussed under detecting concurrent writes, at the cost of additional complexity
The problem is queue latency; the alternative is a faster broker
The problem is storage durability; the alternative is more replicas
There is no alternative to linearizability

questions.explanation: Simplest to understand, not the only option.

questions.question: What is the simplest implementation of linearizability, and why is it rejected?

options.text: Since linearizability essentially means 'behave as though there is only a single copy of the data, and all operations on it are atomic', the simplest answer would be to really only use a single copy of the data — but that approach would not be able to tolerate faults: if the node holding that one copy failed, the data would be lost, or at least inaccessible until the node was brought up again. Hence replication
To use synchronous replication to all replicas; rejected for latency
To use a quorum; rejected for complexity
To use timestamps; rejected for clock skew

questions.explanation: Fault tolerance is what forces replication, which is what makes linearizability hard.

questions.question: Why does the chapter hedge that single-leader replication is only 'potentially linearizable'?

options.text: Because if you make reads from the leader, or from synchronously updated followers, they have the potential to be linearizable — but not every single-leader database is actually linearizable, either by design, for example because it uses snapshot isolation, or due to concurrency bugs
Because leaders always lag their followers
Because single-leader replication cannot be linearizable at all
Because reads must go to followers

questions.explanation: Design choices and bugs both break it in practice.

questions.question: What assumption does using the leader for reads rest on, and what breaks it?

options.text: It relies on the assumption that you know for sure who the leader is. It is quite possible for a node to think that it is the leader when in fact it is not — and if that delusional leader continues to serve requests it is likely to violate linearizability. With asynchronous replication, failover may even lose committed writes, which violates both durability and linearizability
It relies on clock synchronization, which NTP breaks
It relies on quorum size, which rebalancing breaks
It relies on the leader's disk, which crashes break

questions.explanation: Two failure modes: the delusional leader, and lost writes on failover.

questions.question: Why are consensus algorithms listed as flatly linearizable?

options.text: Because consensus protocols bear a resemblance to single-leader replication but contain measures to prevent split brain and stale replicas — thanks to these details, consensus algorithms can implement linearizable storage safely. This is how ZooKeeper and etcd work
Because they use synchronous replication to all nodes
Because they use clock synchronization
Because they avoid leaders entirely

questions.explanation: Split-brain prevention plus stale-replica prevention is the difference from plain single-leader replication.

questions.question: Why is multi-leader replication not linearizable?

options.text: Because systems with multi-leader replication concurrently process writes on multiple nodes and asynchronously replicate them to other nodes, so they can produce conflicting writes that require resolution — such conflicts are an artifact of the lack of a single copy of the data
Because leaders are elected by consensus
Because writes are synchronous across datacenters
Because reads go to followers

questions.explanation: Multiple write-accepting copies contradicts the single-copy illusion by construction.

questions.question: Which things undermine linearizability in Dynamo-style leaderless systems? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Last write wins conflict resolution methods based on time-of-day clocks, as in Cassandra, are almost certainly nonlinearizable, because clock timestamps cannot be guaranteed to be consistent with actual event ordering due to clock skew
Sloppy quorums also ruin any chance of linearizability
Even with strict quorums, nonlinearizable behavior is possible
Read repair, which always restores linearizability

questions.explanation: Depending on the exact configuration of the quorums, and on how you define strong consistency, the claim that quorums give strong consistency is not quite true. A footnote notes that partitioning a single-leader database with a separate leader per partition does not affect linearizability, since it is only a single-object guarantee — though cross-partition transactions are a different matter.

questions.question: Walk Figure 9-6's strict-quorum violation.

options.text: x is initially 0, and a writer updates it to 1 by writing to all three replicas with n = 3 and w = 3. Concurrently, client A reads from a quorum of two nodes with r = 2 and sees the new value 1 on one of the nodes. Also concurrently, client B reads from a different quorum of two nodes and gets back the old value 0 from both. The quorum condition is met, since w plus r is 5 which is greater than n of 3 — yet this execution is nonetheless not linearizable: B's request begins after A's request completes, but B returns the old value while A returns the new value. It's once again the Alice and Bob situation
The quorum condition is violated, which explains the anomaly
Both clients read the same value, so there is no anomaly
The writer only wrote to two replicas

questions.explanation: The quorum condition is satisfied and linearizability still fails, because of variable network delays.

questions.question: What makes strict quorums linearizable, at what cost, and what do Riak and Cassandra do?

options.text: It is possible at the cost of reduced performance: a reader must perform read repair synchronously, before returning results to the application, and a writer must read the latest state of a quorum of nodes before sending its writes. Riak does not perform synchronous read repair due to the performance penalty; Cassandra does wait for read repair to complete on quorum reads, but it loses linearizability if there are multiple concurrent writes to the same key, due to its use of last-write-wins conflict resolution
Both Riak and Cassandra perform synchronous read repair and are linearizable
Neither can be made linearizable under any configuration
Only asynchronous read repair is needed, at no cost

questions.explanation: Synchronous repair on the read path and a read-before-write on the write path.

questions.question: Which operation cannot be made linearizable by these quorum techniques?

options.text: Compare-and-set — only linearizable read and write operations can be implemented that way; a linearizable compare-and-set cannot, because it requires a consensus algorithm. So it is safest to assume that a leaderless system with Dynamo-style replication does not provide linearizability
Read, which requires consensus
Write, which requires a leader
All three operations can be made linearizable

questions.explanation: Compare-and-set is the operation that crosses the line into consensus.

questions.question: In Figure 9-7's two-datacenter deployment with the inter-datacenter link down, what happens with multi-leader replication?

options.text: Each datacenter can continue operating normally: since writes from one datacenter are asynchronously replicated to the other, the writes are simply queued up and exchanged when network connectivity is restored
Both datacenters become unavailable for writes
One datacenter is elected leader and the other becomes read-only
All writes are rejected until the link recovers

questions.explanation: The figure's caption: a network interruption forcing a choice between linearizability and availability.

questions.question: Same interruption, single-leader setup. What happens?

options.text: The leader must be in one of the datacenters, and any writes and any linearizable reads must be sent to the leader. So for any clients connected to a follower datacenter, those read and write requests must be sent synchronously over the network to the leader datacenter — meaning clients connected to the follower datacenter cannot make any writes if the inter-datacenter link is interrupted. They can still make reads from the follower, but those may be stale and hence nonlinearizable, so if the application requires linearizable reads and writes the system becomes unavailable in the datacenters that cannot reach the leader. Clients connected directly to the leader datacenter continue to work normally
Both datacenters continue to accept writes
The follower datacenter is promoted automatically
Reads fail but writes succeed in both datacenters

questions.explanation: Availability survives only where the leader is reachable.

questions.question: State the chapter's two-bullet CAP trade-off and its scope claim.

options.text: If your application requires linearizability and some replicas are disconnected from the other replicas due to a network problem, then some replicas cannot process requests while they are disconnected: they must either wait until the network problem is fixed or return an error — either way they become unavailable. If your application does not require linearizability, then it can be written in a way that each replica can process requests independently, even if it is disconnected from other replicas — in which case the application can remain available in the face of a network problem, but its behavior is not linearizable. The scope: this issue is not just a consequence of single-leader and multi-leader replication — any linearizable database has this problem, no matter how it is implemented, and it isn't specific to multi-datacenter deployments but can occur on any unreliable network, even within one datacenter
The trade-off applies only to multi-datacenter deployments
The trade-off applies only to leaderless replication
The trade-off can be avoided with synchronous replication

questions.explanation: A footnote gives the labels CP — consistent but not available under network partitions — and AP — available but not consistent under network partitions — but notes the classification scheme has several flaws, so it is best avoided.

questions.question: Attribute the CAP theorem, and give its prehistory.

options.text: It was named by Eric Brewer in 2000, although the trade-off has been known to designers of distributed databases since the 1970s
It was proved by Gilbert and Lynch in 2000, with no prehistory
It was named by Brewer in 1990 and proved in 1970
It originates with Codd's relational paper

questions.explanation: Named in 2000, known since the 1970s.

questions.question: What was CAP originally proposed as, and what does the chapter credit it with?

options.text: It was originally proposed as a rule of thumb, without precise definitions, with the goal of starting a discussion about trade-offs in databases. At the time many distributed databases focused on providing linearizable semantics on a cluster of machines with shared storage, and CAP encouraged database engineers to explore a wider design space of distributed shared-nothing systems, which were more suitable for implementing large-scale web services. CAP deserves credit for this culture shift — witness the explosion of new database technologies since the mid-2000s, known as NoSQL
It was proposed as a formal theorem with precise definitions from the start
It was proposed as a product benchmark
It had no influence on database design

questions.explanation: A rule of thumb whose main contribution was a culture shift.

questions.question: Why does the 'Unhelpful CAP Theorem' box reject 'pick 2 out of 3'?

options.text: Because network partitions are a kind of fault, so they aren't something about which you have a choice: they will happen whether you like it or not
Because you can actually pick all three
Because consistency and availability are the same thing
Because the formulation is too technical

questions.explanation: You don't choose whether partitions happen, only what to do when they do.

questions.question: What better phrasing does the box offer?

options.text: At times when the network is working correctly a system can provide both consistency (linearizability) and total availability; when a network fault occurs you have to choose between either linearizability or total availability. So a better way of phrasing CAP would be either Consistent or Available when Partitioned. A more reliable network needs to make this choice less often, but at some point the choice is inevitable
Consistency, Availability, Partition tolerance: pick any two
Choose availability always, since partitions are rare
Choose consistency always, since correctness matters most

questions.explanation: Both when healthy; a forced choice when partitioned.

questions.question: What is the box's second objection, about availability?

options.text: That there are contradictory definitions of the term availability, and the formalization as a theorem does not match its usual meaning — many so-called highly available systems actually do not meet CAP's idiosyncratic definition of availability. Altogether there is a lot of misunderstanding and confusion around CAP, and it does not help us understand systems better, so CAP is best avoided
That availability is impossible to measure
That availability is the same as durability
That availability requires linearizability

questions.explanation: The word does not mean in CAP what it means colloquially.

questions.question: How narrow is the formally defined CAP theorem?

options.text: Very narrow: it considers only one consistency model, namely linearizability, and only one kind of fault, namely network partitions — or more precisely, nodes that are alive but disconnected from each other. It doesn't say anything about network delays, dead nodes, or other trade-offs
It covers all consistency models and all fault types
It covers latency and throughput trade-offs
It covers Byzantine faults

questions.explanation: A footnote disambiguates 'partition': the book normally uses partitioning to mean deliberately breaking down a large dataset into smaller ones (sharding), whereas a network partition is a particular type of network fault, which the book doesn't normally consider separately from other kinds of faults — but since it's the P in CAP, the confusion is unavoidable here.

questions.question: What is the chapter's final verdict on CAP?

options.text: Although CAP has been historically influential, it has little practical value for designing systems: there are many more interesting impossibility results in distributed systems, and CAP has now been superseded by more precise results, so it is of mostly historical interest today
CAP remains the primary design tool for distributed systems
CAP has been proved false
CAP applies only to NoSQL databases

questions.explanation: Historically influential, practically superseded.

questions.question: Give the chapter's most surprising example of a nonlinearizable system.

options.text: Even RAM on a modern multi-core CPU is not linearizable: if a thread running on one CPU core writes to a memory address, and a thread on another CPU core reads the same address shortly afterward, it is not guaranteed to read the value written by the first thread — unless a memory barrier or fence is used
A single-node relational database with serializable isolation
An in-memory key-value store on one machine
A file system on a local disk

questions.explanation: Every CPU core has its own memory cache and store buffer: memory access first goes to the cache by default, and changes are asynchronously written out to main memory. Since accessing data in the cache is much faster than going to main memory, this is essential for good performance — but it means there are several copies of the data, one in main memory and perhaps several more in various caches, which are updated asynchronously, so linearizability is lost.

questions.question: Why is it wrong to invoke CAP to justify the multi-core memory consistency model?

options.text: Because within one computer we usually assume reliable communication, and we don't expect one CPU core to be able to continue operating normally if it is disconnected from the rest of the computer. The reason for dropping linearizability there is performance, not fault tolerance
Because CAP applies only to databases, not CPUs
Because caches are always linearizable
Because CPUs do not partition

questions.explanation: Performance, not fault tolerance. The same is true of many distributed databases that choose not to provide linearizable guarantees: they do so primarily to increase performance, not so much for fault tolerance. The chapter's blunt one-liner: linearizability is slow — and this is true all the time, not only during a network fault.

questions.question: State the Attiya and Welch bound and its consequences.

options.text: They prove that if you want linearizability, the response time of read and write requests is at least proportional to the uncertainty of delays in the network. In a network with highly variable delays, like most computer networks, the response time of linearizable reads and writes is inevitably going to be high. A faster algorithm for linearizability does not exist, but weaker consistency models can be much faster, so this trade-off is important for latency-sensitive systems
They prove linearizability is impossible in asynchronous networks
They prove linearizability costs a constant factor of two
They prove linearizability is free on reliable networks

questions.explanation: Proportional to delay uncertainty, and no faster algorithm exists. Chapter 12 returns to approaches for avoiding linearizability without sacrificing correctness.

questions.question: How does the chapter get from the definition of a linearizable register to a statement about order?

options.text: Because linearizability means behaving as though there is only a single copy of the data and every operation appears to take effect atomically at one point in time, it implies that operations are executed in some well-defined order — which is what the timeline in Figure 9-4 illustrated
Because linearizability requires synchronized clocks, which impose order
Because linearizability requires a leader, who imposes order
Linearizability says nothing about order

questions.explanation: Atomic single points in time compose into a single total order.

questions.question: Which earlier ordering contexts does the chapter recap? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Chapter 5: the main purpose of the leader in single-leader replication is to determine the order of writes in the replication log — if there is no single leader, conflicts can occur due to concurrent operations

Chapter 7: serializability is about ensuring that transactions behave as if they were executed in some sequential order, achieved either by literally executing them serially or by allowing concurrent execution while preventing serialization conflicts
Chapter 8: the use of timestamps and clocks in distributed systems is an attempt to introduce order into a disorderly world, for example to determine which of two writes happened later
Chapter 3: index ordering determines the order of key lookups

questions.explanation: Ordering has been a recurring theme in the book, which suggests it might be an important fundamental idea.

questions.question: Give the Consistent Prefix Reads example and the term for the relationship involved.

options.text: The observer of a conversation saw first the answer to a question, and then the question being answered. This is puzzling because it violates our intuition of cause and effect: if a question is answered, then clearly the question had to be there before the answer, because the person giving the answer must have seen the question. We say that there is a causal dependency between the question and the answer
Two writers set the same key; the term is conflict
A reader sees a stale value; the term is read skew
A write is lost on failover; the term is durability

questions.explanation: Causal dependency is the relationship that ordering must respect.

questions.question: Give the Figure 5-9 multi-leader example and the causal rule it violates.

options.text: Between three leaders, some writes can 'overtake' others due to network delays, so from the perspective of one of the replicas it would look as though there was an update to a row that did not exist. The causal rule: a row must first be created before it can be updated
Two leaders write conflicting values, violating uniqueness
A leader fails and loses writes, violating durability
A follower lags, violating monotonic reads

questions.explanation: Create-before-update is a causal dependency that arrival order can invert.

questions.question: For two operations A and B, what are the three possibilities?

options.text: Either A happened before B, or B happened before A, or A and B are concurrent. If one operation happened before another, the later operation might have known about the earlier one, or built upon it, or depended on it; if two operations are concurrent, neither is aware of the other so there is no causal link between them
Either A is before B or B is before A; concurrency is impossible
Either they conflict or they don't
Either they are on the same node or different nodes

questions.explanation: Three possibilities, of which the third is what makes causality a partial order.

questions.question: What does 'consistent' mean in 'consistent snapshot'?

options.text: It means consistent with causality: if the snapshot contains an answer, it must also contain the question being answered. Observing the entire database at a single point in time makes it consistent with causality, since the effects of all operations that happened causally before that point in time are visible, but no operations that happened causally afterward can be seen. Read skew — non-repeatable reads — means reading data in a state that violates causality
It means all replicas agree on the snapshot
It means the snapshot is linearizable
It means the snapshot has no concurrent writes

questions.explanation: Causal consistency is the precise sense of 'consistent' here.

questions.question: Show write skew as a causality story, and how SSI exploits it.

options.text: Alice was allowed to go off call because the transaction thought that Bob was still on call, and vice versa: they are going off call at the same time, so going off call is causally dependent on the observation of who is currently on call. Serializable snapshot isolation detects write skew by tracking the causal dependencies between transactions
Both wrote the same object, so it is a lost update
Both read stale values, so it is read skew
Write skew has no causal interpretation

questions.explanation: The premise-and-write pattern is a causal dependency, which is exactly what SSI tracks.

questions.question: Restate the Alice/Bob football violation in the language of causality.

options.text: Bob got a stale result from the database after hearing Alice exclaim the result — a causality violation, since Alice's exclamation is causally dependent on the announcement of the score, so Bob should also be able to see the score after hearing about it from Alice. The same pattern appeared again under cross-channel timing dependencies in the guise of an image resizing service
It is a concurrency violation with no causal element
It is a durability violation
It is a write skew

questions.explanation: The out-of-band channel creates the causal dependency the database cannot see.

questions.question: What orderings does causality impose, and what is the causal order?

options.text: Cause comes before effect; a message is sent before that message is received; the question comes before the answer. And like in real life, one thing leads to another: one node reads some data and then writes something as a result, another node reads that written thing and writes something else in turn, and so on. These chains of causally dependent operations define the causal order in the system — that is, what happened before what
Only that writes come before reads
Only that earlier timestamps come before later ones
Only that leaders precede followers

questions.explanation: Chains of dependent operations, not clock readings.

questions.question: Define causal consistency and give an example system providing it.

options.text: If a system obeys the ordering imposed by causality, we say that it is causally consistent. For example, snapshot isolation provides causal consistency: when you read from the database and you see some piece of data, you must also be able to see any data that causally precedes it, assuming it hasn't been deleted in the meantime
Causal consistency means all reads return the latest write; provided by linearizability only
Causal consistency means replicas converge; provided by eventual consistency
Causal consistency means writes are ordered by timestamp; provided by LWW

questions.explanation: Snapshot isolation's causal consistency is what makes its snapshots meaningful.

questions.question: Define total order and partial order with the chapter's examples.

options.text: A total order allows any two elements to be compared, so if you have two elements you can always say which one is greater and which one is smaller — for example natural numbers are totally ordered, since given 5 and 13 you can tell that 13 is greater than 5. In a partial order, sometimes one element is greater than another and sometimes they are incomparable: mathematical sets are partially ordered, since {a, b} is comparable to {a, b, c} because one is a subset of the other, but {a, b} and {b, c} are incomparable because neither is a subset of the other
A partial order allows any two elements to be compared; a total order does not
Both allow all comparisons; they differ in direction
Neither allows comparison of incomparable elements

questions.explanation: A set is greater than another if it contains all the other's elements.

questions.question: Which consistency model gives a total order and which a partial order?

options.text: Linearizability gives a total order: in a linearizable system we have a total order of operations, since the system behaves as if there were only a single copy of the data and every operation is atomic, so for any two operations we can always say which one happened first. Causality gives a partial order: two operations are ordered if they are causally related — one happened before the other — but they are incomparable if they are concurrent
Causality gives a total order; linearizability a partial order
Both give total orders
Both give partial orders

questions.explanation: According to this definition there are no concurrent operations in a linearizable datastore: there must be a single timeline along which all operations are totally ordered. There might be several requests waiting to be handled, but the datastore ensures that every request is handled atomically at a single point in time, acting on a single copy of the data along a single timeline without any concurrency.

questions.question: What does concurrency look like as a picture, and what two illustrations does the chapter offer?

options.text: Concurrency would mean that the timeline branches and merges again, and in that case operations on different branches are incomparable. The chapter offers Figure 5-14, showing a jumble of different operations going on concurrently where the arrows indicate causal dependencies — the partial ordering of operations — and Git, where version histories are very much like a graph of causal dependencies: often one commit happens after another in a straight line, but sometimes you get branches when several people concurrently work on a project, and merges are created when those concurrently created commits are combined
Concurrency is a single line with gaps; the illustration is a replication log
Concurrency is a circle; the illustration is a ring topology
Concurrency cannot be illustrated

questions.explanation: Branch-and-merge is the shape of a partial order.

questions.question: State the relationship between linearizability and causality.

options.text: Linearizability implies causality: any system that is linearizable will preserve causality correctly. In particular, if there are multiple communication channels in a system, linearizability ensures that causality is automatically preserved without the system having to do anything special, such as passing around timestamps between different components — which is what makes linearizable systems simple to understand and appealing
Causality implies linearizability
The two are unrelated
The two are equivalent

questions.explanation: One direction only — linearizability is strictly stronger. But the cost is that making a system linearizable can harm its performance and availability, especially if the system has significant network delays, for example if it's geographically distributed — which is why some distributed data systems have abandoned linearizability, allowing better performance but potentially making them difficult to work with.

questions.question: State the chapter's 'good news' about causal consistency.

options.text: Linearizability is not the only way of preserving causality — a system can be causally consistent without incurring the performance hit of making it linearizable, and in particular the CAP theorem does not apply. In fact causal consistency is the strongest possible consistency model that does not slow down due to network delays, and remains available in the face of network failures. In many cases, systems that appear to require linearizability in fact only really require causal consistency, which can be implemented more efficiently
Causal consistency is weaker than eventual consistency
Causal consistency requires linearizability internally
Causal consistency is the strongest model of all

questions.explanation: Research is exploring this direction, developing databases that preserve causality with performance and availability characteristics similar to eventually consistent systems — but it is quite recent, not much of it has yet made its way into production systems, and there are still challenges to be overcome, though it is a promising direction for future systems.

questions.question: What must a replica do when processing operations, in order to maintain causality?

options.text: In order to maintain causality you need to know which operation happened before which other operation. Concurrent operations may be processed in any order, but if one operation happened before another, then they must be processed in that order on every replica — so when a replica processes an operation, it must ensure that all causally preceding operations have already been processed, and if some preceding operation is missing, the later operation must wait until the preceding operation has been processed
It must process all operations in timestamp order
It must process all operations in arrival order
It may process operations in any order at all

questions.explanation: Wait for missing predecessors is the mechanism.

questions.question: What has to be describable to determine causal dependencies, and what analogy does the chapter use?

options.text: We need some way of describing the 'knowledge' of a node in the system: if a node had already seen the value X when it issued the write Y, then X and Y may be causally related. The analysis uses the kinds of questions you would expect in a criminal investigation of fraud charges: did the CEO know about X at the time when they made decision Y?
Wall-clock timestamps; the analogy is a stopwatch
Network topology; the analogy is a map
Quorum membership; the analogy is a vote

questions.explanation: Knowledge, not timing, is what causality tracks.

questions.question: What does causal consistency require beyond leaderless conflict detection?

options.text: The techniques for determining which operation happened before which are similar to those in Detecting Concurrent Writes, which discussed causality in a leaderless datastore where we need to detect concurrent writes to the same key in order to prevent lost updates — but causal consistency goes further: it needs to track causal dependencies across the entire database, not just for a single key. Version vectors can be generalized to do this
It requires only per-key tracking, like conflict detection
It requires synchronized clocks
It requires a single leader

questions.explanation: Whole-database scope rather than per-key scope.

questions.question: Why does the database need to know which version of the data was read?

options.text: In order to determine the causal ordering, the database needs to know which version of the data was read by the application. This is why in Figure 5-13 the version number from the prior operation is passed back to the database on a write. A similar idea appears in the conflict detection of serializable snapshot isolation: when a transaction wants to commit, the database checks whether the version of the data that it read is still up to date — to that end, the database keeps track of which data has been read by which transaction
To compute the replication lag
To choose which replica to read from
To decide the isolation level

questions.explanation: Passing the read version back is the mechanism in both places.

questions.question: What is the practical objection to tracking all causal dependencies?

options.text: Keeping track of all causal dependencies can become impractical: in many applications clients read lots of data before writing something, and then it is not clear whether the write is causally dependent on all or only some of those prior reads. Explicitly tracking all the data that has been read would mean a large overhead
It requires synchronized clocks, which are unavailable
It requires a single leader, which limits throughput
There is no objection; it is cheap

questions.explanation: Which motivates sequence numbers as a cheaper approximation.

questions.question: Define a logical clock and its properties.

options.text: A better way is to use sequence numbers or timestamps to order events. A timestamp need not come from a time-of-day clock, or physical clock, which have many problems — it can instead come from a logical clock, which is an algorithm to generate a sequence of numbers to identify operations, typically using counters that are incremented for every operation. Such sequence numbers or timestamps are compact, only a few bytes in size, and they provide a total order: you can always compare two sequence numbers to determine which is greater, that is, which operation happened later
A logical clock is a synchronized physical clock with bounded error
A logical clock measures elapsed time in nanoseconds
A logical clock is a vector of per-node timestamps only

questions.explanation: Compact, totally ordered, and independent of physical time.

questions.question: State the promise of 'a total order that is consistent with causality', and the concession.

options.text: You can create sequence numbers in a total order that is consistent with causality: it is promised that if operation A causally happened before B, then A occurs before B in the total order, with A having a lower sequence number than B. Concurrent operations may be ordered arbitrarily. Such a total order captures all the causality information, but it also imposes more ordering than strictly required by causality
It guarantees concurrent operations are left unordered
It captures less causality information than a partial order
It imposes exactly the ordering required by causality

questions.explanation: A footnote gives a useless counterexample: you could generate a random UUID for each operation and compare UUIDs lexicographically to define a total order of operations — that is a valid total order, but the random numbers tell you nothing about which operation actually happened first, or whether the operations were concurrent. A total order that is inconsistent with causality is easy to create, but not very useful.

questions.question: How does a single-leader database get a causally consistent total order for free?

options.text: In a database with single-leader replication, the replication log defines a total order of write operations that is consistent with causality. The leader can simply increment a counter for each operation and thus assign a monotonically increasing sequence number to each operation in the replication log; if a follower applies the writes in the order they appear in the replication log, the state of the follower is always causally consistent, even if it is lagging behind the leader
By synchronizing clocks with NTP
By using version vectors on each write
It cannot; single-leader replication is not causally consistent

questions.explanation: A single sequencing point gives causality for free, even to laggards.

questions.question: Which methods for generating sequence numbers without a single leader does the chapter give? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Each node can generate its own independent set of sequence numbers — for example with two nodes, one can generate only odd numbers and the other only even numbers. More generally you can reserve some bits in the binary representation of the sequence number to contain a unique node identifier, ensuring that two different nodes can never generate the same sequence number

You can attach a timestamp from a time-of-day clock (physical clock) to each operation: such timestamps are not sequential, but if they have sufficiently high resolution they might be sufficient to totally order operations — a fact used in the last write wins conflict resolution method

You can preallocate blocks of sequence numbers: node A might claim the block of sequence numbers from 1 to 1,000, and node B might claim the block from 1,001 to 2,000, so each node can independently assign sequence numbers from its block and allocate a new block when its supply begins to run low
Each node can use a random UUID, which orders causally

questions.explanation: Three methods, all of which scale better than pushing all operations through a single leader.

questions.question: What is the common defect of all three generators, and the specific arguments? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The sequence numbers they generate are not consistent with causality: they do not correctly capture the ordering of operations across different nodes — although each gives a unique, approximately increasing sequence number for each operation

With the odd/even split, one node may end up processing a different number of operations per second than the other, so the counter for even numbers may lag behind the counter for odd numbers, or vice versa — and if you have an odd-numbered operation and an even-numbered operation you cannot accurately tell which one causally happened first
With physical clock timestamps, clock skew means a causally later operation can be assigned a lower timestamp, as in Figure 8-3
With the block allocator, an operation that causally happened later may be assigned a sequence number in the range 1,001 to 2,000 while a causally earlier operation gets one in the range 1 to 1,000

questions.explanation: A footnote notes it is possible to make physical clock timestamps consistent with causality: Google's Spanner estimates the expected clock skew and waits out the uncertainty interval before committing a write, ensuring that a causally later transaction is given a greater timestamp — but most clocks cannot provide the required uncertainty metric.

questions.question: Attribute Lamport timestamps and describe their structure.

options.text: Proposed in 1978 by Leslie Lamport, in what is now one of the most-cited papers in the field of distributed systems. Each node has a unique identifier and each node keeps a counter of the number of operations it has processed, and the Lamport timestamp is then simply a pair of (counter, node ID). Two nodes may sometimes have the same counter value, but by including the node ID in the timestamp each timestamp is made unique. The comparison rule: if you have two timestamps, the one with a greater counter value is the greater timestamp; if the counter values are the same, the one with the greater node ID is the greater timestamp. A Lamport timestamp bears no relationship to a physical time-of-day clock
Proposed in 1998 by Lamport; a single integer counter per system
Proposed in 1978; a vector of counters, one per node
Proposed in 1985; a wall-clock timestamp plus a node ID

questions.explanation: A pair, compared by counter first and node ID as tiebreak.

questions.question: What is 'the key idea about Lamport timestamps' that makes them consistent with causality?

options.text: Every node and every client keeps track of the maximum counter value it has seen so far, and includes that maximum on every request. When a node receives a request or response with a maximum counter value greater than its own counter value, it immediately increases its own counter to that maximum. As long as the maximum counter value is carried along with every operation, this scheme ensures that the ordering from Lamport timestamps is consistent with causality, because every causal dependency results in an increased timestamp
Each node increments its counter only for local operations
Each node synchronizes its counter with NTP
Each node resets its counter on every request

questions.explanation: In Figure 9-8, client A receives a counter value of 5 from node 2 and then sends that maximum of 5 to node 1. At that time node 1's counter was only 1, but it was immediately moved forward to 5, so the next operation had an incremented counter value of 6.

questions.question: Distinguish Lamport timestamps from version vectors.

options.text: They look similar but have a different purpose: version vectors can distinguish whether two operations are concurrent or whether one is causally dependent on the other, whereas Lamport timestamps always enforce a total ordering. From the total ordering of Lamport timestamps you cannot tell whether two operations are concurrent or whether they are causally dependent — the advantage of Lamport timestamps over version vectors is that they are more compact
They are the same thing under two names
Lamport timestamps detect concurrency; version vectors give a total order
Version vectors are more compact than Lamport timestamps

questions.explanation: Total order versus concurrency detection, compactness versus information.

questions.question: Set up the username problem and the apparently sufficient Lamport-timestamp solution.

options.text: A username must uniquely identify a user account, so if two users concurrently try to create an account with the same username, one of the two should succeed and the other should fail. At first glance it seems that a total order of operations should be sufficient to solve this: create an account and take the user with the lower timestamp for the username as the winner, since timestamps are totally ordered this comparison is always valid. This approach works for determining the winner after the fact — once you have collected all the username creation operations in the system
Version vectors are needed rather than Lamport timestamps
Physical timestamps are sufficient
The problem cannot be solved by any ordering

questions.explanation: After-the-fact resolution works; real-time decision-making does not.

questions.question: Why is 'after the fact' not good enough, and what makes the fix unacceptable?

options.text: It is not sufficient when a node has just received a request from a user to create a username and needs to decide right now whether the request should succeed or fail. At that moment the node does not know whether another node is concurrently in the process of creating an account with the same username, and what timestamp that other node may assign to the operation. To be sure that no other node is in the process of concurrently creating an account with the same name and a lower timestamp, you would have to check with every other node to see what it is doing — but if one of the other nodes has failed or cannot be reached due to a network problem, this system would grind to a halt, which is not the kind of fault-tolerant system that we need
The timestamps are not comparable, so the decision is impossible
The fix requires synchronized clocks
It is good enough; no fix is needed

questions.explanation: The root problem: the total order of operations only emerges after you have collected all of the operations. If another node has generated some operations but you don't yet know what they are, you cannot construct the final ordering, because unknown operations from the other node may need to be inserted at various positions in the total order.

questions.question: What extra thing do you need beyond a total ordering?

options.text: To implement something like a uniqueness constraint for usernames it's not sufficient to have a total ordering of operations — you also need to know when that order is finalized. If you have an operation to create a username and you are sure that no other node can insert a claim for the same username ahead of your operation in the total order, then you can safely declare the operation successful. This idea of knowing when your total order is finalized is captured in the topic of total order broadcast
You need synchronized clocks with bounded error
You need version vectors as well as Lamport timestamps
You need nothing more; the total order suffices

questions.explanation: Finality, not just order, is the missing requirement.

questions.question: How does single-leader replication produce a total order, and what two challenges follow?

options.text: By choosing one node as the leader and sequencing all operations on a single CPU core on the leader. The challenge is how to scale the system if the throughput is greater than a single leader can handle, and how to handle failover if the leader fails. In the distributed systems literature this problem is known as total order broadcast or atomic broadcast
By synchronizing clocks; the challenges are drift and skew
By quorum voting; the challenges are latency and availability
By version vectors; the challenges are size and comparison

questions.explanation: A footnote objects that 'atomic broadcast' is a confusing term because it is inconsistent with other uses of the word atomic: it has nothing to do with atomicity in ACID transactions and is only indirectly related to atomic operations or atomic registers. Total order multicast is another synonym.

questions.question: Give total order broadcast's two safety properties.

options.text: Reliable delivery: no messages are lost — if a message is delivered to one node, it is delivered to all nodes. Totally ordered delivery: messages are delivered to every node in the same order
Bounded delivery and ordered acknowledgment
At-most-once delivery and causal ordering
Exactly-once delivery and timestamp ordering

questions.explanation: A correct algorithm for total order broadcast must ensure the reliability and ordering properties are always satisfied, even if a node or the network is faulty: of course messages will not be delivered while the network is interrupted, but an algorithm can keep retrying so that the messages get through when the network is eventually repaired, and then they must still be delivered in the correct order.

questions.question: Which systems implement total order broadcast, and what does the chapter take that as a hint of?

options.text: ZooKeeper and etcd — a hint that there is a strong connection between total order broadcast and consensus
Kafka and RabbitMQ — a hint about message queues
Cassandra and Riak — a hint about leaderless replication
PostgreSQL and MySQL — a hint about replication logs

questions.explanation: The systems that implement consensus are exactly the ones that implement total order broadcast.

questions.question: Why is total order broadcast exactly what you need for database replication?

options.text: Because if every message represents a write to the database, and every replica processes the same writes in the same order, then the replicas will remain consistent with each other, aside from any temporary replication lag. This principle is known as state machine replication, returned to in Chapter 11
Because it guarantees bounded replication lag
Because it eliminates the need for a leader
Because it makes writes idempotent

questions.explanation: Similarly, it can implement serializable transactions: if every message represents a deterministic transaction to be executed as a stored procedure, and if every node processes those messages in the same order, then the partitions and replicas of the database are kept consistent with each other.

questions.question: What property about when the order is fixed makes total order broadcast stronger than timestamp ordering?

options.text: With total order broadcast the order is fixed at the time the messages are delivered: a node is not allowed to retroactively insert a message into an earlier position in the order if subsequent messages have already been delivered. This fact makes total order broadcast stronger than timestamp ordering. Another way of looking at it is that total order broadcast is a way of creating a log, as in a replication log, transaction log or write-ahead log: delivering a message is like appending to the log, and since all nodes must deliver the same messages in the same order, all nodes can read the log and see the same sequence of messages
The order is fixed at send time, not delivery time
