The order is never fixed, which makes it flexible
The order is fixed by timestamps, making it equivalent

questions.explanation: Finality at delivery is precisely what Lamport timestamps lack.

questions.question: How does total order broadcast implement a lock service with fencing tokens?

options.text: Every request to acquire the lock is appended as a message to the log, and all messages are sequentially numbered in the order they appear in the log. The sequence number can then serve as a fencing token, because it is monotonically increasing. In ZooKeeper this sequence number is called zxid
Locks are granted by timestamp comparison, with the timestamp as the token
Locks require a separate consensus round per acquisition
Total order broadcast cannot implement locks

questions.explanation: Log position doubles as a monotonic fencing token.

questions.question: Is linearizability the same as total order broadcast?

options.text: Not quite, but there are close links between the two. Total order broadcast is asynchronous: messages are guaranteed to be delivered reliably in a fixed order, but there is no guarantee about when a message will be delivered, so one recipient may lag behind the others. By contrast, linearizability is a recency guarantee: a read is guaranteed to see the latest value written
Yes, they are identical
No, and they are unrelated
Total order broadcast is a recency guarantee; linearizability is asynchronous

questions.explanation: A footnote ranks them formally: a linearizable read-write register is an 'easier' problem, because total order broadcast is equivalent to consensus, which has no deterministic solution in the asynchronous crash-stop model, whereas a linearizable read-write register can be implemented in the same system model. However, supporting atomic operations such as compare-and-set or increment-and-get in a register makes it equivalent to consensus — so the problems of consensus and a linearizable register are closely related.

questions.question: Give the algorithm for implementing a linearizable compare-and-set using total order broadcast. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Append a message to the log, tentatively indicating the username you want to claim
Read the log, and wait for the message you appended to be delivered back to you

Check for any messages claiming the username that you want. If the first message for your desired username is your own, then you are successful: you can commit the username claim, perhaps by appending another message to the log, and acknowledge it to the client. If the first message for your desired username is from another user, you abort the operation
Query all other nodes before appending, to check for concurrent claims

questions.explanation: A footnote notes that if you don't wait but acknowledge the write immediately after it has been enqueued, you get something similar to the memory consistency model of multi-core x86 processors — which is neither linearizable nor sequentially consistent.

questions.question: Why is the append-and-check procedure correct?

options.text: Because log entries are delivered to all nodes in the same order, so if there are several concurrent writes, all nodes will agree on which one came first. Choosing the first of the conflicting writes as the winner and aborting later ones ensures that all nodes agree on whether a write was committed or aborted. A similar approach can be used to implement serializable multi-object transactions on top of a log
Because the log is synchronized by clocks
Because each node checks with every other node
Because the log is single-node

questions.explanation: Shared order plus first-wins gives agreement without further coordination.

questions.question: Which options for linearizable reads on top of a log does the chapter give? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Sequence reads through the log: append a message, read the log, and perform the actual read when the message is delivered back to you — the message's position in the log thus defines the point in time at which the read happens. Quorum reads in etcd work somewhat like this

If the log allows you to fetch the position of the latest log message in a linearizable way, you can query that position, wait for all entries up to that position to be delivered to you, and then perform the read — this is the idea behind ZooKeeper's sync() operation
You can make your read from a replica that is synchronously updated on writes, and is thus sure to be up to date — a technique used in chain replication
You can read from any replica, since total order broadcast guarantees recency

questions.explanation: Three options. The last is wrong because total order broadcast is asynchronous and gives no recency guarantee.

questions.question: To build total order broadcast from linearizable storage, what do you need and what is the algorithm?

options.text: You need a linearizable register that stores an integer and has an atomic increment-and-get operation, or an atomic compare-and-set. The algorithm: for every message you want to send through total order broadcast, increment-and-get the linearizable integer, then attach the value you got from the register as a sequence number to the message; you can then send the message to all nodes, resending any lost messages, and the recipients deliver the messages consecutively by sequence number
You need a synchronized clock and a timestamp per message
You need a version vector per node
You need a single leader, which defeats the purpose

questions.explanation: A linearizable counter gives gapless, agreed sequence numbers.

questions.question: A node has delivered message 4 and receives message 6. What does it do, and what does this illustrate?

options.text: Unlike Lamport timestamps, the numbers from the linearizable counter form a sequence with no gaps — so if a node has delivered message 4 and receives an incoming message with a sequence number of 6, it knows that it must wait for message 5 before it can deliver message 6. The same is not the case with Lamport timestamps; in fact, this is the key difference between total order broadcast and timestamp ordering
It delivers message 6 immediately, since order is per-node
It discards message 6 as out of order
It requests message 5 from the sender and then reorders

questions.explanation: Gaplessness is what lets a node know when its order is final.

questions.question: How hard is it to make a linearizable integer with an atomic increment-and-get operation?

options.text: As usual, if things never failed it would be easy: you could just keep it in a variable on one node. The problem lies in handling the situation when network connections to that node are interrupted, and restoring the value when that node fails. In general, if you think hard enough about linearizable sequence number generators, you inevitably end up with a consensus algorithm
It is trivial in all cases; a single variable suffices
It is impossible under any system model
It requires only a synchronized clock

questions.explanation: It is proved that a linearizable compare-and-set (or increment-and-get) register and total order broadcast are both equivalent to consensus: if you can solve one of these problems, you can transform it into a solution for the others. The chapter calls this quite a profound and surprising insight.

questions.question: State the informal goal of consensus and the warning attached to it.

options.text: Consensus is one of the most important and fundamental problems in distributed computing. On the surface it seems simple: informally, the goal is to get several nodes to agree on something. You might think this shouldn't be too hard — but unfortunately, many broken systems have been built in the mistaken belief that this problem is easy to solve
The goal is to order all operations; the warning is about performance
The goal is to detect failures; the warning is about clocks
The goal is to replicate data; the warning is about durability

questions.explanation: Deceptively simple, with a long record of broken implementations.

questions.question: Why does consensus appear so late in the book?

options.text: Because although consensus is very important, the topic is quite subtle, and appreciating the subtleties requires some prerequisite knowledge: replication (Chapter 5), transactions (Chapter 7), system models (Chapter 8), linearizability, and total order broadcast (this chapter). Even in the academic research community, the understanding of consensus only gradually crystallized over the course of decades, with many misunderstandings along the way
Because it is less important than the earlier topics
Because it was only invented recently
Because the author wanted to end on a hard note

questions.explanation: Five prerequisites, and decades of gradual crystallization even among researchers.

questions.question: Why does single-leader replication need consensus?

options.text: Because all nodes need to agree on which node is the leader. The leadership position might become contested if some nodes can't communicate with others due to a network fault, so consensus is important here to avoid a bad failover resulting in split brain in which two nodes both believe themselves to be the leader — if there were two leaders they would both accept writes and their data would diverge, leading to inconsistency and data loss
Because followers must agree on the order of writes
Because clients must agree on which replica to read from
It doesn't; single-leader replication never needs consensus

questions.explanation: Agreement on leadership identity is the consensus instance here.

questions.question: State the atomic commit problem as an instance of consensus.

options.text: In a database that supports transactions spanning several nodes or partitions, we have the problem that a transaction may fail on some nodes but succeed on others. If we want to maintain transaction atomicity in the ACID sense, we have to get all nodes to agree on the outcome of the transaction: either they all abort or roll back if anything goes wrong, or they all commit if nothing goes wrong. This instance of consensus is known as the atomic commit problem
Nodes must agree on the isolation level for each transaction
Nodes must agree on the order of writes within a transaction
Nodes must agree on which partition holds each row

questions.explanation: A footnote distinguishes them formally: atomic commit is formalized slightly differently from consensus — an atomic transaction can commit only if all participants vote to commit and must abort if any participant needs to abort, whereas consensus is allowed to decide on any value that is proposed by one of the participants. However, atomic commit and consensus are reducible to each other, and nonblocking atomic commit is harder than consensus.

questions.question: State the FLP result and resolve the apparent contradiction.

options.text: Fischer, Lynch and Paterson prove that there is no algorithm that is always able to reach consensus if there is a risk that a node may crash — which seems to contradict the rest of the section, since in a distributed system we must assume that nodes may crash. The resolution: the FLP result is proved in the asynchronous system model, a very restrictive model that assumes a deterministic algorithm that cannot use any clocks or timeouts. If the algorithm is allowed to use timeouts, or some other way of identifying suspected crashed nodes — even if the suspicion is sometimes wrong — then consensus becomes solvable. Even just allowing the algorithm to use random numbers is sufficient to get around the impossibility result. So although the FLP result about the impossibility of consensus is of great theoretical importance, distributed systems can usually achieve consensus in practice
FLP is simply wrong and has been disproved
FLP applies to the partially synchronous model, so consensus is impossible in practice
FLP applies only to Byzantine faults

questions.explanation: The impossibility is real, and the model it holds in is not the one real systems live in.

questions.question: What verdict does the chapter pre-announce about two-phase commit?

options.text: That 2PC is the most common way of solving atomic commit and is implemented in various databases, messaging systems and application servers — and that 2PC is a kind of consensus algorithm, but not a very good one. By learning from 2PC the chapter works toward better consensus algorithms, such as those used in ZooKeeper (Zab) and etcd (Raft)
That 2PC is the best available consensus algorithm
That 2PC is not a consensus algorithm at all
That 2PC has been superseded and is no longer used

questions.explanation: A consensus algorithm, but not a good one.

questions.question: Describe how a single node implements atomic commit.

options.text: Atomicity is commonly implemented by the storage engine: when a client asks the database node to commit the transaction, the database makes the transaction's writes durable — typically in a write-ahead log — and then appends a commit record to the log on disk. If the database crashes in the middle of this process, the transaction is recovered from the log when the node restarts: if the commit record was successfully written to disk before the crash the transaction is considered committed; if not, any writes from that transaction are rolled back. Thus on a single node transaction commitment crucially depends on the order in which data is durably written to disk: first the data, then the commit record. The key deciding moment is the instant at which the disk finishes writing the commit record — before that moment it is still possible to abort, but after it the transaction is committed. What makes it atomic is that the commit is decided by a single device: the controller of one particular disk drive, attached to one particular node
By taking a lock on every row and releasing it at commit
By writing the commit record first and then the data
By voting among the storage engine's threads

questions.explanation: A single device deciding at a single instant is what makes single-node commit atomic.

questions.question: Give the two examples of multi-node transactions and who supports them.

options.text: A multi-object transaction in a partitioned database, or a term-partitioned secondary index where the index entry may be on a different node from the primary data. Most 'NoSQL' distributed datastores do not support such distributed transactions, but various clustered relational systems do
Replication and partitioning; all NoSQL stores support them
Batch and stream processing; only Hadoop supports them
Reads and writes; all databases support them

questions.explanation: Cross-partition writes and global secondary indexes are the two shapes.

questions.question: Why is it not sufficient to send a commit request to all nodes and commit independently on each? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Some nodes may detect a constraint violation or conflict, making an abort necessary, while other nodes are successfully able to commit
Some of the commit requests might be lost in the network, eventually aborting due to a timeout, while other commit requests get through
Some nodes may crash before the commit record is fully written and roll back on recovery, while others successfully commit
The nodes would deadlock waiting for each other

questions.explanation: If some nodes commit the transaction but others abort it, the nodes become inconsistent with each other, as in Figure 7-3.

questions.question: State the rule about commits and why it holds.

options.text: A node must only commit once it is certain that all other nodes in the transaction are also going to commit. A transaction commit must be irrevocable — you are not allowed to change your mind and retroactively abort a transaction after it has been committed. The reason is that once data has been committed it becomes visible to other transactions, and thus other clients may start relying on that data: this principle forms the basis of read committed isolation. If a transaction were allowed to abort after committing, any transactions that read the committed data would be based on data that was retroactively declared not to have existed — so they would have to be reverted as well
A node may commit independently and abort later if needed
Commits are revocable within a bounded window
Commits must be confirmed by a majority before becoming visible

questions.explanation: The chapter concedes one escape: it is possible for the effects of an already-committed transaction to be undone by another, compensating transaction — but from the database's point of view this is a separate transaction, and thus any cross-transaction correctness requirements are the application's problem.

questions.question: Define two-phase commit and where it is exposed.

options.text: 2PC is an algorithm for achieving atomic transaction commit across multiple nodes — that is, to ensure that either all nodes commit or all nodes abort. It is a classic algorithm in distributed databases, used internally in some databases and also made available to applications in the form of XA transactions, supported by the Java Transaction API, or via WS-AtomicTransaction for SOAP web services. The name comes from the fact that it is split into two phases
2PC is an isolation level exposed through SQL
2PC is a replication protocol exposed through the replication log
2PC is a locking protocol exposed through FOR UPDATE

questions.explanation: A box warns: two-phase commit (2PC) and two-phase locking are two very different things. 2PC provides atomic commit in a distributed database whereas 2PL provides serializable isolation — they are entirely separate concepts, so ignore the unfortunate similarity in the names.

questions.question: What new component does 2PC introduce, and how is it deployed?

options.text: A coordinator, also known as a transaction manager. The coordinator is often implemented as a library within the same application process that is requesting the transaction — for example embedded in a Java EE container — but it can also be a separate process or service. Examples include Narayana, JOTM, BTM and MSDTC
A quorum of voters, always deployed as a separate cluster
A leader elected among the participants
A message broker between the participants

questions.explanation: Often a library in the application process, which turns out to matter a great deal for availability.

questions.question: Walk the basic 2PC flow.

options.text: A 2PC transaction begins with the application reading and writing data on multiple database nodes, as normal — these nodes are called participants in the transaction. When the application is ready to commit, the coordinator begins phase 1: it sends a prepare request to each of the nodes, asking them whether they are able to commit, and then tracks the responses. If all participants reply 'yes', indicating they are ready to commit, the coordinator sends out a commit request in phase 2 and the commit actually takes place. If any of the participants replies 'no', the coordinator sends an abort request to all nodes in phase 2
The coordinator commits on one node first, then propagates
The participants vote among themselves with no coordinator
The coordinator sends commit requests immediately and aborts later if needed

questions.explanation: Prepare, then decide, then commit or abort.

questions.question: Give the chapter's marriage analogy.

options.text: The minister asks the bride and groom individually whether each wants to marry the other, and typically receives the answer 'I do' from both. After receiving both acknowledgments the minister pronounces the couple husband and wife — the transaction is committed, and the happy fact is broadcast to all attendees. If either bride or groom does not say 'yes', the ceremony is aborted. On the second half: after saying 'I do' you cannot retract that statement — if you faint after saying 'I do' and you don't hear the minister speak the words 'You are now husband and wife', that doesn't change the fact that the transaction was committed. When you recover consciousness later you can find out whether you are married by querying the minister for the status of your global transaction ID, or you can wait for the minister's next retry of the commit request, since the retries will have continued throughout your period of unconsciousness
The minister marries the couple first and asks afterward
Each partner may retract consent at any time
The guests vote on whether the marriage proceeds

questions.explanation: The fainting bit is the analogue of a participant crashing after voting yes.

questions.question: Give the first three steps of the detailed 2PC breakdown. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: When the application wants to begin a distributed transaction, it requests a transaction ID from the coordinator, which is globally unique

The application begins a single-node transaction on each of the participants, and attaches the globally unique transaction ID to it; all reads and writes are done in one of these single-node transactions. If anything goes wrong at this stage, the coordinator or any of the participants can abort

When the application is ready to commit, the coordinator sends a prepare request to all participants, tagged with the global transaction ID; if any of these requests fails or times out, the coordinator sends an abort request for that transaction ID to all participants
The coordinator asks the participants to vote among themselves before phase 1

questions.explanation: Setup, normal work, then the prepare round.

questions.question: Give the last three steps, including the commit point. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: When a participant receives the prepare request, it makes sure that it can definitely commit the transaction under all circumstances — writing all transaction data to disk, since a crash, a power failure, or running out of disk space is not an acceptable excuse for refusing to commit later, and checking for any conflicts or constraint violations. By replying 'yes' it promises to commit the transaction without error if requested, thereby surrendering the right to abort the transaction but without actually committing it

When the coordinator has received responses to all prepare requests, it makes a definitive decision, committing only if all participants voted 'yes'; it must write that decision to its transaction log on disk so that it knows which way it decided in case it subsequently crashes. This is called the commit point

Once the coordinator's decision has been written to disk, the commit or abort request is sent to all participants; if this request fails or times out, the coordinator must retry forever until it succeeds — there is no more going back, and if the decision was to commit, that decision must be enforced no matter how many retries it takes. If a participant has crashed in the meantime, the transaction will be committed when it recovers, since the participant voted 'yes' and cannot refuse to commit when it recovers
If a participant crashes before the commit request arrives, the coordinator aborts the transaction on the remaining nodes

questions.explanation: The protocol has two crucial points of no return: when a participant votes 'yes' it promises that it will definitely be able to commit later, even though the coordinator may still choose to abort; and once the coordinator decides, that decision is irrevocable. Those promises ensure the atomicity of 2PC — single-node atomic commit lumps these two events into one, writing the commit record to the transaction log.

questions.question: What are the two cases of coordinator failure, and what is the resulting participant state called?

options.text: If the coordinator fails before sending the prepare requests, a participant can safely abort the transaction. But once a participant has received a prepare request and voted 'yes', it can no longer abort unilaterally — it must wait to hear back from the coordinator whether the transaction was committed or aborted. If the coordinator crashes or the network fails at this point, the participant can do nothing but wait: a participant's transaction in this state is called in doubt or uncertain
Either the coordinator aborts or commits; the state is called pending
Either it fails before or after commit; the state is called blocked
There is only one case; the state is called prepared

questions.explanation: Without hearing from the coordinator the participant has no way of knowing whether the transaction was committed or aborted — in principle the participants could communicate among themselves, but that is not part of the 2PC protocol.

questions.question: Walk Figure 9-10 and prove that neither unilateral choice is safe.

options.text: The coordinator actually decided to commit, and database 2 received the commit request — but the coordinator crashed before it could send the commit request to database 1, so database 1 does not know whether to commit or abort. If database 1 unilaterally aborts it will end up inconsistent with database 2, which has committed. And it is not safe to unilaterally commit either, because another participant may have aborted
Both databases received the commit request, so no ambiguity arises
Database 1 can safely abort after a timeout
Database 1 can safely commit after a timeout

questions.explanation: The only way 2PC can complete is by waiting for the coordinator to recover. This is why the coordinator must write its commit or abort decision to a transaction log on disk before sending commit or abort requests: when it recovers, it determines the status of all in-doubt transactions by reading its transaction log, and any transactions that don't have a commit record in the coordinator's log are aborted. Thus the commit point of 2PC comes down to a regular single-node atomic commit on the coordinator.

questions.question: Why is 2PC called a blocking atomic commit protocol, and what does the chapter say about 3PC?

options.text: Because 2PC can become stuck waiting for the coordinator to recover. In theory it is possible to make an atomic commit protocol nonblocking, so that it does not get stuck if a node fails — but making this work in practice is not so straightforward. As an alternative to 2PC, an algorithm called three-phase commit has been proposed, but 3PC assumes a network with bounded delay and nodes with bounded response times, and in most practical systems with unbounded network delay and process pauses it cannot guarantee atomicity
Because it holds locks; 3PC removes the locks and solves the problem
Because it requires unanimity; 3PC requires only a majority
Because it has two phases; 3PC adds a phase and is now standard

questions.explanation: Nonblocking atomic commit requires a perfect failure detector — a reliable mechanism for telling whether a node has crashed or not — and in a network with unbounded delay a timeout is not a reliable failure detector, since a request may time out due to a network problem even if no node has crashed. For this reason 2PC continues to be used, despite the known problem with coordinator failure.

questions.question: Quantify the performance cost of distributed transactions.

options.text: Distributed transactions in MySQL are reported to be over 10 times slower than single-node transactions, so it is not surprising when people advise against using them. Much of the performance cost inherent in two-phase commit is due to the additional disk forcing (fsync) required for crash recovery, and the additional network round-trips
About 10% slower, mainly due to network latency
About twice as slow, due to locking
No slower; the cost is purely operational

questions.explanation: Many cloud services choose not to implement distributed transactions due to the operational problems they engender: they have a mixed reputation, on the one hand seen as providing an important safety guarantee that would be hard to achieve otherwise, and on the other criticized for causing operational problems, killing performance, and promising more than they can deliver.

questions.question: Name and define the two kinds of distributed transaction the chapter says are often conflated.

options.text: Database-internal distributed transactions: some distributed databases such as VoltDB and MySQL Cluster's NDB storage engine support internal transactions among the nodes of that database, in which case all the nodes participating in the transaction are running the same database software. And heterogeneous distributed transactions: the participants are two or more different technologies — for example two databases from different vendors, or even non-database systems such as message brokers — in which a distributed transaction across these systems must ensure atomic commit even though the systems may be entirely different under the hood
Local and remote transactions, distinguished by network hops
Read-only and read-write transactions
Single-partition and cross-partition transactions

questions.explanation: Database-internal transactions do not have to be compatible with any other system, so they can use any protocol and apply optimizations specific to that particular technology — and can often work quite well. On the other hand, transactions spanning heterogeneous technologies are a lot more challenging.

questions.question: Explain how heterogeneous distributed transactions give exactly-once message processing, and what breaks it.

options.text: Message queues and databases can be tied together: a message from a queue can be acknowledged as processed if and only if the database transaction for processing the message was successfully committed. This is implemented by atomically committing the message acknowledgment and the database writes in a single transaction, even if the message broker and the database are two unrelated technologies running on different machines. If either the message delivery or the database transaction fails, both are aborted, and the message broker may safely redeliver the message later — so by atomically committing the message and the side effects of its processing, the message is effectively processed exactly once even if it required a few retries, since the abort discards any side effects of the partially completed transaction. But this only works if all systems affected by the transaction are able to use the same atomic commit protocol: if a side effect of processing a message is to send an email and the email server does not support two-phase commit, it could happen that the email is sent two or more times if message processing fails and is retried
It works by deduplicating messages at the application level
It works by making all message processing idempotent
It cannot be done at all

questions.explanation: The guarantee holds only for participants that speak the same commit protocol.

questions.question: Expand XA, date it, and name its supporting systems.

options.text: X/Open XA, short for eXtended Architecture, is a standard for implementing two-phase commit across heterogeneous technologies, introduced in 1991 and widely implemented. It is supported by many traditional relational databases — PostgreSQL, MySQL, DB2, SQL Server and Oracle — and message brokers including ActiveMQ, HornetQ, MSMQ and IBM MQ
eXtensible Atomic protocol, from 2001, supported only by Java EE containers
X/Open Atomic, from 1981, supported only by mainframe databases
eXactly-once Architecture, from 1999, supported by message brokers only

questions.explanation: XA is not a network protocol — it is merely a C API for interfacing with a transaction coordinator, with bindings in other languages. In Java EE the API is the Java Transaction API (JTA), which in turn is supported by many drivers for databases using JDBC and drivers for message brokers using the JMS APIs.

questions.question: Where does the XA coordinator live, and what happens when the application process dies?

options.text: The transaction coordinator implements the XA API, but the standard does not specify how it should be implemented — in practice it is often simply a library that is loaded into the same process as the application issuing the transaction, rather than a separate service. It keeps track of the participants in a transaction, collects participants' responses after asking them to prepare, and uses a log on the local disk to keep track of the commit/abort decision for each transaction. If the application process crashes, or the machine on which the application is running dies, the coordinator goes with it: any participants with prepared but uncommitted transactions are then stuck in doubt. Since the coordinator's log is on the application server's local disk, that server must be restarted and the coordinator library must read the log to recover the commit/abort outcome of each transaction — only then can the coordinator use the database driver's XA callbacks to ask participants to commit or abort as appropriate. The database server cannot contact the coordinator directly, since all communication must go via its client library
The coordinator runs as a replicated service, so an application crash is harmless
The coordinator runs inside the database, so it survives application crashes
The coordinator is stateless, so no recovery is needed

questions.explanation: A library on the application server's disk becomes a critical piece of durable state.

questions.question: Why can't the rest of the system simply ignore an in-doubt transaction?

options.text: The problem is with locking: database transactions usually take a row-level exclusive lock on any rows they modify, to prevent dirty writes, and in addition, if you want serializable isolation a database using two-phase locking would also have to take a shared lock on any rows read by the transaction. The database cannot release those locks until the transaction commits or aborts — shown as a shaded area in Figure 9-9 — so when using two-phase commit, a transaction must hold onto the locks throughout the time it is in doubt
Because in-doubt transactions consume memory
Because in-doubt transactions block replication
They can be ignored; in-doubt transactions are harmless

questions.explanation: If the coordinator has crashed and takes 20 minutes to start up again, those locks will be held for 20 minutes; and if the coordinator's log is entirely lost for some reason, those locks will be held forever, or at least until the situation is manually resolved by an administrator. While those locks are held no other transaction can modify those rows, and depending on the database other transactions may even be blocked from reading them — so large parts of your application can become unavailable until the in-doubt transaction is resolved.

questions.question: What are orphaned in-doubt transactions, and why doesn't rebooting help?

options.text: They are transactions for which the coordinator cannot decide the outcome for whatever reason — for example because the transaction log has been lost or corrupted due to a software bug. These transactions cannot be resolved automatically, so they sit forever in the database holding locks and blocking other transactions. Even rebooting your database servers will not fix this problem, since a correct implementation of 2PC must preserve the locks of an in-doubt transaction even across restarts; otherwise it would risk violating the atomicity guarantee. It's a sticky situation. The only way out is for an administrator to manually decide whether to commit or roll back the transactions, examining the participants of each in-doubt transaction, determining whether any participant has committed or aborted already, and then applying the same outcome to the other participants — which is potentially a lot of manual effort, most likely to be needed under high stress and time pressure during a serious production outage
They are transactions with no participants; rebooting clears them
They are aborted transactions that were never cleaned up; a vacuum process removes them
They are duplicated transactions; deduplication resolves them

questions.explanation: Preserving the locks across restarts is required for correctness, which is exactly why rebooting cannot help.

questions.question: Define heuristic decisions and decode the euphemism.

options.text: Many XA implementations have an emergency escape hatch called heuristic decisions, allowing a participant to unilaterally decide to abort or commit an in-doubt transaction without a definitive decision from the coordinator. Heuristic here is a euphemism for probably breaking atomicity, since it violates the system of promises in two-phase commit — so heuristic decisions are intended only for getting out of catastrophic situations, and not for regular use
They are optimizations that speed up the common case
They are automatic retries with exponential backoff
They are coordinator elections after a crash

questions.explanation: 'Heuristic' means 'probably breaking atomicity'.

questions.question: What is the 'key realization' about the coordinator, and what limitations follow? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The transaction coordinator is itself a kind of database — one that stores the outcome of transactions — and so it needs to be approached with the same care as any other important database

If the coordinator is not replicated but runs only on a single machine, it is a single point of failure for the entire system, yet surprisingly many coordinator implementations are not highly available by default or have only rudimentary replication support

Many server-side applications are developed in a stateless model, with all persistent state stored in a database, which has the advantage that application servers can be added and removed at will — but when the coordinator is part of the application server, it changes the nature of the deployment: the coordinator's logs become a crucial part of the durable system state, as important as the databases themselves, since they are required in order to recover in-doubt transactions after a crash. Such application servers are no longer stateless
The coordinator must be co-located with the database for performance

questions.explanation: The coordinator is a database, a single point of failure, and a destroyer of statelessness.

questions.question: Give limitations 3 and 4 of XA.

options.text: Since XA needs to be compatible with a wide range of data systems, it is necessarily a lowest common denominator: for example it cannot detect deadlocks across different systems, since that would require a standardized protocol for systems to exchange information on the locks that each transaction is waiting for, and it does not work with SSI, since that would require a protocol for identifying conflicts across different systems. And for 2PC to successfully commit a transaction all participants must respond, so if any part of the system is broken the transaction also fails — distributed transactions thus have a tendency of amplifying failures, which runs counter to our goal of building fault-tolerant systems
XA is too fast for reliable logging, and it requires special hardware
XA cannot support more than two participants, and it requires synchronized clocks
XA requires Byzantine fault tolerance, and it forbids replication

questions.explanation: For database-internal distributed transactions the limitations are not so great — a distributed version of SSI is possible, for example. However, there remains the problem that for 2PC to commit, all participants must respond. The chapter notes there are alternative methods that achieve the same thing without the pain of heterogeneous distributed transactions, returning to them in Chapters 11 and 12.

questions.question: Give the informal and formal statements of consensus.

options.text: Informally, consensus means getting several nodes to agree on something — for example if several people concurrently try to book the last seat on an airplane, or the same seat in a theater, or try to register an account with the same username, a consensus algorithm could be used to determine which one of these mutually incompatible operations should be the winner. Formally, one or more nodes may propose values, and the consensus algorithm decides on one of those values: in the seat-booking example, when several customers are concurrently trying to buy the last seat, each node handling a customer request may propose the ID of the customer it is serving, and the decision indicates which one of those customers got the seat
Formally, all nodes must propose the same value and the algorithm confirms it
Formally, the algorithm invents a new value not proposed by anyone
Formally, each node decides independently and they are later reconciled

questions.explanation: Proposals in, one decision out.

questions.question: Name and define the four properties a consensus algorithm must satisfy. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Uniform agreement: no two nodes decide differently
Integrity: no node decides twice
Validity: if a node decides value v, then v was proposed by some node
Termination: every node that does not crash eventually decides some value

questions.explanation: The chapter notes this is the formalization of 'uniform consensus', equivalent to regular consensus in asynchronous systems with unreliable failure detectors — and that the literature usually refers to processes rather than nodes, but the book uses nodes for consistency.

questions.question: Which properties define the core idea of consensus, and what is validity actually for?

options.text: The uniform agreement and integrity properties define the core idea of consensus: everyone decides on the same outcome, and once you have decided you cannot change your mind. The validity property exists mostly to rule out trivial solutions — for example an algorithm that always decides null no matter what was proposed would satisfy the agreement and integrity properties, but not the validity property
Termination and validity are the core; agreement rules out trivial solutions
Validity is the core; agreement is an optimization
All four are equally core with no distinction

questions.explanation: If you don't care about fault tolerance, satisfying the first three properties is easy: you can just hardcode one node to be the 'dictator' and let that node make all of the decisions — but if that one node fails, the system can no longer make any decisions. This is, in fact, what we saw in the case of two-phase commit: if the coordinator fails, in-doubt participants cannot decide whether to commit or abort.

questions.question: What does termination formalize, and which algorithm fails it?

options.text: Termination formalizes the idea of fault tolerance: it essentially says that a consensus algorithm cannot simply sit around and do nothing forever — it must make progress, so even if some nodes fail the other nodes must still reach a decision. Termination is a liveness property, whereas the other three are safety properties. The system model assumes that when a node crashes it suddenly disappears and never comes back: you must assume that your node is buried under 30 feet of mud and is never going to come back online, so any algorithm that has to wait for a node to recover is not going to be able to satisfy the termination property — in particular, 2PC does not meet the requirements for termination
Termination formalizes safety; 2PC satisfies it
Termination formalizes ordering; Paxos fails it
Termination formalizes durability; no algorithm fails it

questions.explanation: Liveness, with a crash-stop assumption that rules out waiting for recovery.

questions.question: How many nodes must survive for consensus?

options.text: Of course, if all nodes crash and none of them are running, then it is not possible for any algorithm to decide anything — so there is a limit to the number of failures an algorithm can tolerate. In fact it can be proved that any consensus algorithm requires at least a majority of nodes to be functioning correctly in order to assure termination, and that majority can safely form a quorum. Thus the termination property is subject to the assumption that fewer than half of the nodes are crashed or unreachable
At least one node, which can decide alone
All nodes must survive
At least two-thirds of nodes, in the non-Byzantine case

questions.explanation: Most implementations ensure that the safety properties — agreement, integrity and validity — are always met, even if a majority of nodes fail or there is a severe network problem: so a large-scale outage can stop the system from being able to process requests, but it cannot corrupt the consensus system by causing it to make invalid decisions.

questions.question: What fault model do most consensus algorithms assume, and what is the bound for the harder model?

options.text: Most consensus algorithms assume that there are no Byzantine faults — if a node does not correctly follow the protocol, for example if it sends contradictory messages to different nodes, it may break the safety properties of the protocol. It is possible to make consensus robust against Byzantine faults as long as fewer than one-third of the nodes are Byzantine-faulty, but the chapter says it doesn't have space to discuss those algorithms in detail
They assume Byzantine faults, tolerating up to one-half faulty nodes
They assume no faults at all
They assume crash-stop faults with no bound

questions.explanation: Non-Byzantine by default, with a one-third bound if you want Byzantine tolerance.

questions.question: Name the best-known fault-tolerant consensus algorithms, and what do they actually decide?

options.text: Viewstamped Replication (VSR), Paxos, Raft and Zab. There are quite a few similarities between these algorithms, but they are not the same. Most of them don't directly use the formal model of proposing and deciding on a single value: instead they decide on a sequence of values, which makes them total order broadcast algorithms — and deciding on a sequence of values is equivalent to performing several rounds of consensus, where in each round nodes propose the message that they want to send next and then decide on the next message to be delivered in the total order. So total order broadcast is equivalent to repeated rounds of consensus
Only Paxos and Raft, which decide a single value each time
2PC and 3PC, which decide commit or abort
Gossip and anti-entropy, which decide replica state

questions.explanation: Viewstamped Replication, Raft and Zab implement total order broadcast directly, because that is more efficient than doing repeated rounds of one-value-at-a-time consensus; in the case of Paxos this optimization is known as Multi-Paxos. The chapter advises against implementing a consensus system yourself — which is probably not advisable, it's hard.

questions.question: Map the four consensus properties onto the total order broadcast guarantees they produce. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Agreement: all nodes decide to deliver the same messages in the same order
Integrity: messages are not duplicated
Validity: messages are not corrupted and not fabricated out of thin air
Termination: messages are not lost

questions.explanation: A clean one-to-one mapping between consensus properties and broadcast guarantees.

questions.question: Why didn't Chapter 5 need consensus, and what conundrum does automatic failover create?

options.text: It comes down to how the leader is chosen: if the leader is manually chosen and configured by the humans in your operations team you essentially have a 'consensus algorithm' of the dictatorial variety, where only one node is allowed to accept writes — and if that node goes down, the system becomes unavailable for writes until the operators manually configure a different node to be the leader. Such a system can work well in practice, but it does not satisfy the termination property of consensus, because it requires human intervention in order to make progress. Automatic failover brings us closer to fault-tolerant total order broadcast, and hence to solving consensus — but there is a problem: we need consensus in order to elect a leader, yet total order broadcast algorithms all look like single-leader replication and so require a leader. It seems that in order to elect a leader we first need a leader; in order to solve consensus, we must first solve consensus
Chapter 5 used consensus implicitly through quorums
Automatic failover avoids consensus entirely
Manual failover satisfies termination

questions.explanation: The apparent circularity is resolved by epoch numbers.

questions.question: What weaker guarantee do the protocols make about leaders, and what is the epoch number called in each algorithm?

options.text: All of these protocols internally use a leader in some form or another, but they don't guarantee that the leader is unique: instead they make a weaker guarantee — the protocols define an epoch number, guaranteeing that within each epoch the leader is unique. It is called the ballot number in Paxos, view number in Viewstamped Replication, and term number in Raft
They guarantee a unique leader at all times; the number is the sequence number
They guarantee no leader; the number is the round number
The epoch number is called the zxid in all three

questions.explanation: Uniqueness per epoch rather than globally is what breaks the circularity.

questions.question: How do epoch numbers advance, and what is the tie-break rule?

options.text: Every time the current leader is thought to be dead, a vote is started among the nodes to elect a new leader, and this election is given an incremented epoch number. Thus epoch numbers are totally ordered and monotonically increasing. If there is a conflict between two different leaders in two different epochs — which may happen if the previous leader actually wasn't dead after all — then the leader with the higher epoch number prevails. Before a leader is allowed to decide anything, it must first check that there isn't some other leader with a higher epoch number which might take a conflicting decision
Epoch numbers are assigned randomly, and the lower one prevails
Epoch numbers come from wall-clock time, and the later one prevails
Epoch numbers never change once assigned

questions.explanation: Monotonic epochs with higher-wins resolution.

questions.question: Why can't a node simply trust that it is the leader?

options.text: Because a node cannot necessarily trust its own judgment — just because a node thinks that it is the leader, that does not necessarily mean the other nodes accept it as their leader. So instead it must collect votes from a quorum of nodes: for every decision that a leader wants to make, it must send the proposed value to the other nodes and wait for a quorum of nodes to respond in favor of the proposal. The quorum typically, but not always, consists of a majority of nodes, and a node votes in favor of a proposal only if it is not aware of any other leader with a higher epoch
Because leaders are elected by timestamp
Because leadership is transferred on every write
It can trust itself; leadership is self-certifying

questions.explanation: Majority acceptance, not self-assertion, is what confers leadership.

questions.question: Walk the quorum-overlap argument.

options.text: There are two rounds of voting: once to choose a leader, and a second time to vote on a leader's proposal. The key insight is that the quorums for those two votes must overlap — so if a vote on a proposal succeeds, at least one of the nodes that voted for it must have also participated in the most recent leader election. Thus if the vote on a proposal does not reveal any higher-numbered epoch, the current leader can conclude that no leader election with a higher epoch number has happened, and therefore be sure that it still holds the leadership; it can then safely decide the proposed value
The two quorums must be disjoint to avoid bias
Only one round of voting is needed
The quorums must be unanimous

questions.explanation: Overlap is what lets a successful proposal vote certify continued leadership.

questions.question: How does epoch voting differ from two-phase commit? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: In 2PC the coordinator is not elected
Fault-tolerant consensus algorithms only require votes from a majority of nodes, whereas 2PC requires a 'yes' vote from every participant
Consensus algorithms define a recovery process by which nodes can get into a consistent state after a new leader is elected, ensuring that the safety properties are always met
2PC uses epoch numbers while consensus algorithms do not

questions.explanation: These differences are key to the correctness and fault tolerance of a consensus algorithm.

questions.question: What do consensus algorithms deliver, and what are the first two costs?

options.text: They bring concrete safety properties — agreement, integrity and validity — to systems where everything else is uncertain, and they remain fault-tolerant, able to make progress as long as a majority of nodes are working and reachable. They provide total order broadcast, and therefore they can also implement linearizable atomic operations in a fault-tolerant way. Cost one: the process by which nodes vote on proposals before they are decided is a kind of synchronous replication — databases are often configured to use asynchronous replication, in which case some committed data can potentially be lost on failover, but many people choose to accept this risk for the sake of better performance. Cost two: consensus systems always require a strict majority to operate, so you need a minimum of three nodes in order to tolerate one failure, since the remaining two out of three form a majority, or a minimum of five nodes to tolerate two failures, since the remaining three out of five form a majority — and if a network failure cuts off some nodes from the rest, only the majority portion of the network can make progress, and the rest is blocked
They provide eventual consistency with no majority requirement
They require only two nodes to tolerate one failure
They are fully asynchronous with no replication cost

questions.explanation: Safety plus fault tolerance, paid for in synchronous voting and majority quorums.

questions.question: Give the remaining limitations of consensus algorithms. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Static membership: most consensus algorithms assume a fixed set of nodes that participate in voting, which means you can't just add or remove nodes in the cluster. Dynamic membership extensions allow the set of nodes to change over time, but they are much less well understood than static membership algorithms

Timeout sensitivity: consensus systems rely on timeouts to detect failed nodes, and in environments with highly variable network delays — especially geographically distributed systems — it often happens that a node falsely believes the leader to have failed due to a transient network issue. Although this error does not harm the safety properties, frequent leader elections result in terrible performance, because the system can end up spending more time choosing a leader than doing any useful work

Network-fault sensitivity: Raft in particular has been shown to have unpleasant edge cases — if the entire network is working correctly except for one particular network link that is consistently unreliable, Raft can get into situations where leadership continually bounces between two nodes, or the current leader is continually forced to resign, so the system effectively never makes progress
Byzantine sensitivity: consensus algorithms break if any node is slow

questions.explanation: Three further limitations: membership, timeouts and pathological link failures. Other consensus algorithms have been designed to be more robust to unreliable networks.

questions.question: How are ZooKeeper and etcd usually described, and what question does the chapter pose about them?

options.text: They are often described as 'distributed key-value stores' or 'coordination and configuration services', and their API looks pretty much like that of a database: you can read and write the value for a given key, and iterate over keys. So if they're basically databases, why do they go to all the effort of implementing a consensus algorithm? What makes them different from any other kind of database?
They are described as message brokers; the question is about ordering
They are described as relational databases; the question is about SQL
They are described as caches; the question is about eviction

questions.explanation: You rarely need to use ZooKeeper directly, since it is actually not well suited as a general-purpose database — it's more likely that you will end up relying on it indirectly via some other project, for example HBase, Hadoop YARN, OpenStack Nova and Kafka all rely on ZooKeeper running in the background.

questions.question: What is ZooKeeper's data-size design point, and how is it replicated?

options.text: ZooKeeper and etcd are designed to hold small amounts of data that can fit entirely in memory, although they still write to disk for durability — so you wouldn't want to store all of your application's data here. That small amount of data is replicated across all the nodes using a fault-tolerant total order broadcast algorithm, which is just what you need for database replication: if each message represents a write to the database, applying the same writes in the same order keeps replicas consistent with each other
They hold terabytes on disk, replicated by quorum writes
They hold data in memory only, with no durability
They hold arbitrary data, replicated asynchronously

questions.explanation: ZooKeeper is modeled after Google's Chubby lock service and implements not only total order broadcast, and hence consensus, but also an interesting set of other features that turn out to be particularly useful when building distributed systems: linearizable atomic operations, total ordering of operations, failure detection and change notifications.

questions.question: Which primitive gives you a lock, and under what conditions does the guarantee hold?

options.text: Using an atomic compare-and-set operation you can implement a lock: if several nodes concurrently try to perform the same operation, only one of them will succeed. The consensus protocol guarantees that the operation will be atomic and linearizable, even if a node fails or the network is interrupted at any point. A distributed lock is usually implemented as a lease, which has an expiry time so that it is eventually released in case the client fails
A read-write register, guaranteed only when the network is healthy
A timestamp comparison, guaranteed only with synchronized clocks
A quorum read, guaranteed only with strict quorums

questions.explanation: Compare-and-set is exactly the operation that requires consensus.

questions.question: Why do you need a fencing token, and how does ZooKeeper supply it?

options.text: When some resource is protected by a lock or lease, you need a fencing token to prevent clients from conflicting with each other in the case of a process pause. The fencing token is some number that monotonically increases every time the lock is acquired, and ZooKeeper provides this by totally ordering all operations and giving each operation a monotonically increasing transaction ID (zxid) and version number (cversion)
Tokens prevent replay attacks; ZooKeeper uses cryptographic nonces
Tokens identify clients; ZooKeeper uses session IDs
Tokens are not needed with leases

questions.explanation: Monotonic ordering of all operations is what makes zxid a valid fencing token.

questions.question: Describe the ZooKeeper session and failure detection mechanism.

options.text: Clients maintain a long-lived session on ZooKeeper servers, and the client and server periodically exchange heartbeats to check that the other node is still alive. Even if the connection is temporarily interrupted, or a ZooKeeper node fails, the session remains active — but if the heartbeats cease for a duration that is longer than the session timeout, ZooKeeper declares the session to be dead. Any locks held by a session can be configured to be automatically released when the session times out; ZooKeeper calls these ephemeral nodes
Clients poll on every operation; there is no session concept
The server pings clients once per hour; locks are never released automatically
Sessions end immediately on any connection interruption

questions.explanation: Sessions survive transient interruption but not sustained heartbeat loss.

questions.question: What can a client do beyond reading another client's values?

options.text: Not only can one client read locks and values that were created by another client, but it can also watch them for changes — so a client can find out when another client joins the cluster, based on the value it writes to ZooKeeper, or if another client fails, because its session times out and its ephemeral nodes disappear. By subscribing to notifications a client avoids having to frequently poll to find out about changes
It can only poll; watches are not supported
It can subscribe but only to its own keys
It can receive notifications only at session end

questions.explanation: Of ZooKeeper's four features, only the linearizable atomic operations really require consensus — however, it is the combination of these features that makes systems like ZooKeeper so useful for distributed coordination.

questions.question: Which use cases does the chapter give where the ZooKeeper/Chubby model works well? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Allocating work to nodes: if you have several instances of a process or service and one of them needs to be chosen as leader or primary, and if the leader fails one of the other nodes should take over — useful for single-leader databases but also for job schedulers and similar stateful systems
Deciding which partition to assign to which node when you have some partitioned resource — a database, message streams, file storage, distributed actor system and so on

Rebalancing: as new nodes join the cluster some partitions need to be moved from existing nodes to the new nodes in order to rebalance the load, and as nodes are removed or fail other nodes need to take over the failed nodes' work
Storing the application's primary dataset

questions.explanation: These tasks can be achieved by judicious use of atomic operations, ephemeral nodes and notifications in ZooKeeper — and if done correctly, this approach allows the application to automatically recover from faults without human intervention. It's not easy, despite the appearance of libraries such as Apache Curator that provide higher-level tools on top of the ZooKeeper client API, but it is still much better than attempting to implement the necessary consensus algorithms from scratch, which has a poor success record.

questions.question: An application grows to thousands of nodes. Why can't the coordination mechanism grow with it?

options.text: Because trying to perform majority votes over so many nodes would be terribly inefficient — instead ZooKeeper runs on a fixed number of nodes, usually three or five, and performs its majority votes among those nodes while supporting a potentially large number of clients. Thus ZooKeeper provides a way of 'outsourcing' some of the work of coordinating nodes — consensus, operation ordering and failure detection — to an external service
Because ZooKeeper has a hard limit of 100 nodes
Because clients cannot connect to more than three nodes
It can grow; ZooKeeper scales its voting set with the cluster

questions.explanation: A small fixed voting set serving many clients is the architectural answer.

questions.question: What kind of data belongs in ZooKeeper, and what doesn't?

options.text: Normally the kind of data managed by ZooKeeper is quite slow-changing: it represents information like 'the node running on 10.1.1.23 is the leader for partition 7', which may change on a timescale of minutes or hours. It is not intended for storing the runtime state of the application, which may change thousands or even millions of times per second — if application state needs to be replicated from one node to another, other tools such as Apache BookKeeper can be used
High-frequency runtime state belongs in ZooKeeper; slow-changing metadata does not
Both kinds belong in ZooKeeper
Neither kind belongs in ZooKeeper

questions.explanation: Minutes-to-hours metadata, not millions-per-second state.

questions.question: Does service discovery require consensus?

options.text: ZooKeeper, etcd and Consul are also often used for service discovery — finding out which IP address you need to connect to in order to reach a particular service. In cloud datacenter environments where it is common for virtual machines to continually come and go you often don't know the IP addresses of your services ahead of time, so services can be configured such that when they start up they register their network endpoints in a service registry. However, it is less clear whether service discovery actually requires consensus: DNS is the traditional way of looking up the IP address for a service name, and it uses multiple layers of caching to achieve good performance and availability. Reads from DNS are absolutely not linearizable, and it is usually not considered problematic if the results from a DNS query are a little stale — it is more important that DNS is reliably available and robust to network interruptions
Yes, service discovery strictly requires linearizability
No, and neither does leader election
Yes, because IP addresses must be unique

questions.explanation: Although service discovery does not require consensus, leader election does — so if your consensus system already knows who the leader is, it can make sense to also use that information to help other services discover who the leader is. For this purpose some consensus systems support read-only caching replicas, which asynchronously receive the log of all decisions of the consensus algorithm but do not actively participate in voting, and are therefore able to serve read requests that do not need to be linearizable.

questions.question: Define a membership service and explain how it gets around the Chapter 8 obstacle.

options.text: A membership service determines which nodes are currently active and live members of a cluster. Due to unbounded network delays it's not possible to reliably detect whether another node has failed — however, if you couple failure detection with consensus, nodes can come to an agreement about which nodes should be considered alive or not. It could still happen that a node is incorrectly declared dead by consensus even though it is actually alive, but it is nevertheless very useful for a system to have agreement on which nodes constitute the current membership: for example choosing a leader could mean simply choosing the lowest-numbered among the current members, and this approach would not work if different nodes have divergent opinions on who the current members are
A membership service detects failures perfectly using timeouts
A membership service avoids consensus by using gossip
A membership service requires synchronized clocks

questions.explanation: Agreement without accuracy is still valuable. Research into membership services goes back to the 1980s and has been important for building highly reliable systems, for example for air traffic control.

questions.question: Which six problems does the Summary say are equivalent to consensus? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Linearizable compare-and-set registers, which must atomically decide whether to set their value based on whether the current value equals the parameter given in the operation; and atomic transaction commit, where a database must decide whether to commit or abort a distributed transaction
Total order broadcast, where the messaging system must decide on the order in which to deliver messages

Locks and leases, where when several clients are racing to grab a lock or lease the lock decides which one successfully acquired it; and membership/coordination service, where given a failure detector such as timeouts the system must decide which nodes are alive and which should be considered dead because their sessions timed out

Uniqueness constraint, where when several transactions concurrently try to create conflicting records with the same key the constraint must decide which one to allow and which should fail with a constraint violation

questions.explanation: Six problems, equivalent in the sense that if you have a solution for one of them, you can easily transform it into a solution for one of the others. Achieving consensus means deciding something in such a way that all nodes agree on what was decided, and such that the decision is irrevocable.

questions.question: Under what conditions are all six problems straightforward?

options.text: All of these are straightforward if you only have a single node, or if you are willing to assign the decision-making capability to a single node. This is what happens in a single-leader database: all the power to make decisions is vested in the leader, which is why such databases are able to provide linearizable operations, uniqueness constraints, a totally ordered replication log, and more. But if that single leader fails, or if a network interruption makes the leader unreachable, such a system becomes unable to make any progress
When a majority of nodes agree, with no leader needed
When clocks are synchronized to within one millisecond
When the network is reliable

questions.explanation: Vesting decisions in one node makes them easy and makes that node a single point of failure.

questions.question: Give the three ways to handle leader failure and the objections. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Wait for the leader to recover, and accept that the system will be blocked in the meantime — many XA/JTA transaction coordinators choose this option. But it does not fully solve consensus because it does not satisfy the termination property: if the leader does not recover, the system can be blocked forever

Manually fail over by getting humans to choose a new leader node and reconfigure the system to use it — an option taken by many relational databases. It is a kind of consensus by 'act of God', since the human operator outside of the computer system makes the decision, and the speed of failover is limited by the speed at which humans can act, which is generally slower than computers
Use an algorithm to automatically choose a new leader, which requires a consensus algorithm — and it is advisable to use a proven algorithm that correctly handles adverse network conditions
Allow multiple leaders and resolve conflicts afterward, which fully solves consensus

questions.explanation: Wait, human, or algorithm — and only the third satisfies termination.

questions.question: A single-leader database provides linearizability without running consensus on every write. So why does it still require consensus?

options.text: Because although a single-leader database can provide linearizability without executing a consensus algorithm on every write, it still requires consensus to maintain its leadership and for leadership changes. So in some sense, having a leader only 'kicks the can down the road': consensus is still required, only in a different place, and less frequently
It does not require consensus at all
It requires consensus on every write after all
It requires consensus only for reads

questions.explanation: Consensus relocated and made rare, not eliminated. In order to elect a leader, we first need a leader.

questions.question: How does the Summary characterize ZooKeeper's role?

options.text: Tools like ZooKeeper play an important role in providing an 'outsourced' consensus, failure detection and membership service that applications can use. It's not easy to use, but it is much better than trying to develop your own algorithms that can withstand all the problems discussed in Chapter 8. If you find yourself wanting to do one of those things that is reducible to consensus, and you want it to be fault-tolerant, then it is advisable to use something like ZooKeeper
As a general-purpose database that replaces relational systems
As a message broker for high-throughput streams
As a library you should reimplement yourself for your use case

questions.explanation: Hard to use, much better than the alternative of rolling your own.
